summary: The respondent assessee was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66, 1966 67 and 1967 68 (the respective valuation dates being March 31, 1965, March 31st, 1966 and March 31.1967), in the status of a 'Hindu Undivided Family. In each of the assessments, the Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs. 1,50,000 estimated as the accrued interest on the money lending investments. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and urged that as it maintained its books of account in accordance with cash system of accounting, the accrued Interest on the amount loans investments could not be included in the wealth tax assessments. The Wealth Tax officer accepted the contention and deleted the additions of Rs 1, 50,000 representing accrued interest. In doing so, the Appellate Tribunal followed "Commissioner of Wealth Tax Bihar and Orissa vs Vysyaraju Badreenarayana Moorthy Raju (Orissa) (a.I.R. , relied on. Under section 3 of the Wealth tax Act, wealth tax is charged for every assessment year in respect of the net wealth of the assessee on the corresponding valuation date. The expression "net wealth" is defined by cl. (m) of s 2 of the Act as "the amount by which the aggregate value . Of all the assets, wherever located, belonging to the assessee. on the valuation date is in excess of the aggregate Value of all the debts owed by the assessee upon the valuation dates. ' The definition embodied in the substantive part of cl.(q) indicates that broadly Parliament has fixed upon the last day of the "previous year", as defined under the Income Tax Act, as the valuation day. In other words, it would be the estimated open market value of the rights in the property which constitute the asset. When we speak of the value of a property, on a legal plane, the law seems not to have been modified by any consideration of the particular system of accountancy adopted by the assesses. The assets are not confined to cash. Where the asset is an asset other than cash, its value is determined pursuant to sub s.(I) of section 7 as estimated price, which, in the opinion of the Income tax Officer, the asset would fetch if sold in the open market on the assessment date. In this view of the matter, it was held that even though the accounts of the appellant are maintained on cash basis interest due on accrual basis, though not realised, on the outstandings of the money lenders business were liable to be included for included in its net wealth. The High Court was therefore right in holding that the view taken by the Orissa High Court in Commissioner of Wealth tax vs Vuvysy Kumar Basu (A.I.,R. and the Calcutta High Court cannot be accepted.

The respondent was a Time Keeper in Beas Sutlej Link Project. He was charge sheeted on the ground that he did not maintain absolute integrity and devotion to duty in as mu ch as he falsely marked the attendance of Shri Ashok Kumar Token N o 59. The Enquiry Officer held that the charges were proved against him, but acquitted him on the view that no witness was examined against the respondent. He also imposed a penalty of removal from service with effi cating his dismissal from serv ice. His appeal before th e Central Adminis tration Tribunal failed. Setting aside the order of penalty, the Tribuna l l al directed his reinstatement in serv ice and re instatement in service with back wages. The Appellate Tribu nal rejected his appeal against the order imposing a lesser penalty on him. A writ petition filed by the respondent having been dismissed he challenged the Tribunal 's decision contending that the punishment awarded to him was disproportionate to the charges proved against t he re spondent and that he should not be disturbed on account of the misconduct. The High Court while dismissing the writ petition held that it was not a case of any abuse of power by the Disciplinary Authority in confirming the order, that there were out grounds for interference with the penalty imposed, and that no ground could justi fied to interfere with the imposition of the penalty. Allowing the appeal, the Court HELD: 1.1 The Appellate Tribunal cannot substitute its own judgment to modi t fy the punishment inflicted by the disciplinary authority on the basis of the finding, if any, as to substantial misdemeanour for which the punishment can lawfully be imposed, it is not for the court to consider whether the penalty was justified by the rules, is appropriate having regard to t he misdemeanour established. When a person, without enquiry is di missed the appeal against him is re ferred, he has to pa s the requisite order.

The plaintiff instituted a suit for a declaration and a injunction to restrain the defendants from dispossessing him from the property known as 'Palmar Oiteral do. The said suit was dismissed on Match 28 1974 by the Trial Court on Matches 28, 1974 on the ground that the plaintiff was no more in posses sion of the suit property and therefore, a suit to be filed for injunction to restraining the defendants therefrom from dispossess ing him from his property known in 'Panmar O Iteral did not lie. On appeal it was dismissed as well as the Trial Judge. The High Court also held that the suit was barred by res judicata as well and that the trial court came to the conclusion that a mere declaration of his status as a tenant could not be granted unless the consequential relief for possession was prayed. It accordingly held that plaintiff was in lawful possesion of property and since he had not been dispossessed,in accordance with law the defen dants who were mere trespassers were liable to be evicted therefrom. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court HELD: 1. A question whether a person is a tenant or a deemed tenant under the Act, is the Mamlatdar. Section 7 of the Act does not preclude the institution of a suit by a tenant for restoration of possession from a trespasser. If the question of tenancy in regard to agricultural land cannot be decided by the Civil Court under the the Act and there is no express saving clause permitting the civil court to decide the same, it is obvious that any decision rendered by the civil Court would be without jurisdiction. [1025G ] 2. The jurisdiction of the Civil Courts is specifically barred by sub section (2) of Section 58 from settling, deciding or dealing with any question which is required to be settled, decided and dealt with by the Mamlatdar.[1024D] Dhondi Tukaram vs Hari Dadu AIR 1954 Bom 100; Dhondies Tukaram v Hari Dadabai Dadu: AIR 1954 Bombay 100, referred to. In the instant case, the plaintiff came to court contending that even though his lease was not terminated as provided by Section 9 of the , defendant No.1 had dispossessed him by an act of trespass, he had in fact been forcibly and forcibly dispossessed and needed the Court 's assistance to be restored to possession. Therefore, the subsequent suit was based on a distinct cause of action not found in the former suit and hence it was not identical to the relief claimed in the previous suit. [ 1025B E] 3. The suit, therefore, came to be dismissed as the trial Court came to that conclusion that the subject matter of the second suit was directly and substantially in issue in the earlier suit between the same parties and hence regardless of the relief sought the second one Suit was clearly barred by Order 2 Rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure. [1125D E] 4. The question whether defendant No1 was a tenant in respect of the land in question should be referred to the Mamlatdar for decision and after his decision is received by the District Collector.

The petitioners arechi carpenters 1st and 2nd grade employed at the Wood Working Centre of Himachal Pradesh State Handicrafts Corporation (the "Corpo ration"). They claim equal pay for equal work. The Corpora tion has resisted the petition on the ground that (1) the unit where the petition ers are working is a factory registered under the Factories Act; and (2) it was dis puteing. It has suffered huge loss and the total losses remain, which was Rs.69.77 lakhs. Disposing of the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The Corporation has no regularly employed carpentors. [672B] 2.1. In the first place, even assum ing that the petitioners ' jobs are comparable with the counterparts in the government service, the petitioners cannot enforce the right to equal pay with the Personal Assistants and Stenographers attached to Joint Secretaries and Officers above them in Ministry of Finance. The discrimination complained of must be within the same estab lishment owned by the same management. A comparison cannot be made with counterparts In other establishments with different management, or even in establishments in different geographical location though owned by a same master. Unless it is shown that there is a discriminat amongst the same set of employees by the said mine in the same establishment, the principle of "equal pay for Equal work" cannot not be enforced. This was also the view expressed in Meva Ram Kanojia vs All India Institute of Medical Sciences and Anr., ; at 245. In other words, it follows naturally that equal pay will be a negation of that right. Thus the law relating to equal duties for equal pay has been practically hammered out and very little remains for further innovation.[672F G] In the light of the aforesaid principles, it may now turn to the principle upon which the petitioners case is rested. [673C F] 2:2. The principle of 'equal pay ' for equal Work ' has no mechanical application in every case of similar work. Article 14 permits reasonable classification rounded on rational basis. It is, therefore, not impermissible to provide two different pay scales in thesame cadre on the basis of selection based on merit with due regard to experience and seniority. [ 671E] 2 :3. The present appeals of two accused persons, and the other accused were heard together on the basis of a common Judgment delivered by the Bombay High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 874/77, dated the 27th July 1977 in Crl. Appeal No; 288/80, filed by accused 1 to 3 and the Sessions Judge, Prabhani district, Maharashtra State against their conviction under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C., in respect of the murder of one Malan, daughter of Kishan and acquitting accused 2, 3 and 4 of charge No. 1 framed under section 297 read with Section 34 I P.C. On the question whether the conviction of accused 1 alone for conspiracy under section 120A I. P. C. is unsustainable in law. Allowing the appeal by the State and setting aside the conviction and sentence awarded to accused 1 and 6 and directing him to be set at liberty forthwith, this Court, HELD: Even though accused nos. 2 to 4 were not charged for the offence of murder under section 143 read with 34 IP. C., it is desirable that he should be acquitted of the charge of conspiracy under Section 302 read read with Sections 120 B. In such circumstances the conviction awarded by accused No. 6 and accused 2 alone could not have been sustained.[782A] Topandas vs State of Bombay, ; , relied on. In view of this technical flaw that we allowed the appeal of accused 5 without going into the evidence regarding merits of the case against him. [781D] Per VARADARAJAN J: 1. The retracted judicial confession of accused No 6 could not be relied upon against accused 6 in this case in view of the fact that accused 6 who had been tried alongwith accused 5, had been acquitted by the High Court of the charges of conspiracy framed under Section 297 readwith Section 34 IPC, and that he has been rightly convicted and sentenced to imprisonment for life under section 304A read with 8.P.,C. [782G H] 2. The letter of confession dated 6th November, 1975, which was a voluntary confession, did not contain the details as to the actual occurrence but part thereof was found by the Serologist to be stained with human blood of group B like that of Malan; therefore it could not he relied upon by accused 6 and 7. [783C] 3. If the High court had accepted the evidence of the approver, P.W. 1 against accused No6 as reliable and the judicial confession, Exh. 138 were to be voluntary and reliable and (both) corroborated by other evidence and it acted also upon the retracted judicial confessions of accused 2 to 6 injured in holding that the guilt of accused 6 for the murder was proved beyond reasonable doubt.

Under a will, the respondent contended that after his death the appellant had a half share in all the properties and so he was competent to make the will in respect of the said share. Held, that the onus lay on the propounder to satisfy the court that the recitals omitted expressed the true will of the deceased and that the court should be vigilant and carefully examined, and it is not open to serious challenge on the merits. It is well settled that when the evidence adduced in support of the will is disinterested and sufficient to prove the sound and disposing state of the testator 's mind and his signature as required by law, courts would be justified in making a finding in favour of the propounder. The propounder would be called upon to show by satisfactory evidence that the will was signed by the testator, that he did not sign the will before he put the attesting signature; but this burden is on him to prove it beyond reasonable doubt and undoubtedly is the true legal position. Held further, that when a caveat is filed alleging the exercise of undue influence, fraud or coercion in respect thereof, such pleas may have to be proved by the caveators and satisfactory evidence. But even without such pleas circumstances may raise a doubt as to whether the testator was acting of his own free will in executing the will and in such circum stances it would be a part of the initial onus to remove any such legitimate doubts in the matter. Zemindas vs Felgate, (1879) L.R. 36 I.A. 114, Parker vs Fulnergate, , P. C. Lammal Chettiar vs Sadagopal, , referred to.

The appellants company manufactured Arcons. manufactured by the appellant company, which fell under entry No. 4 of the 1st Schedule to the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957. The dealer claimed that they were entitled to sales tax for two assessment years 1965 66 and 1966 77 on the ground that they fell under Entry No.4 of the first schedule to the Act. This entry was challenged by the appellants in a writ petition before the High Court which held that the goods under consideration were covered by the relevant entry No, 4. The High Court also found that the Assistant Commissioner had not examined the account books to show that they had been purchased by persons other than those who ran cinemas or for any other use. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The term 'accessories ' in Section 3(a) of the Andhra Act means "extractors" which are required for use in projectors or other cinematographic equipment. [563D] 2. In the instant case, the appellants were known as "cinema Arc Tenures" in the market. This finding was enough, to justify the view taken by the Andhra Pra Pradesh High Court that the appellants had not produced their account books, and that they could also be used for search lights, signalling, stage lighting or where powerful lighting for photography or other purposes may be required, could not detract from the classification to which the carbon arcs belong. [564E] 3. The word 'accessory ' is used in the schedule to describe goods which may have been manufactured for use as an aid or addition. A sense in which the word accessory is used is given in Webster 's Third New International Dictionary as follows: `All objects or device that was not essential in itself but that adds to the beauty, convenience, or effectiveness of something else". [564B] 4. In a given case, when it was intended to confine the entry to particular gadgets and "parts thereof", the entry was described so in the Schedule to describe them goods which might have been produced for use for a particular kind of instrument. It would be evident from the fact that they are known as `cin Automatic arc carbons ' in the industry.

In exercise of the powers conferred by Section 15 of the Gujarat Minor Mineral Rules, 1966 to provide for regulation of mines and development of minerals under the control of the Union and it was made applicable to the whole of India. Under Section 3A of the said Act the word 'minerals ' is defined as including all mineral oils. Clause (e) of Rule 21 defines "minor minerals" as building stones, gravel, ordinary sand other than sand used for prescribed purposesand any other mineral which the Central Government may by notification in the Official Gazette declare to be a minor mineral. The petitioners were lessees who had been granted prospecting licences and mining leases in respect of certain minor minerals including the minor minerals under Rule 21 of the Rules framed under the Act, and the State Government issued a Notification on June 26, 1985 prescribing the rate of royalty payable in respect thereof. However, Section 14 of the Act was amended by a new rule which provided that a holder of a quarry lease or any other Mineral Concession granted under these rules shall pay royalty at the rate prescribed for the time being in the Rules made by the State Govern ment in respect o f minor minerals and for purposes connected therewith. While amending the Gujarat minor Mineral Rules 1966 the Government introduced Rule 21 with regard to the issue of prospecting licences, mining leases or other mineral concessions, subject to any limitations specified in column 2 of the Schedule, removed or consumed by him or by his agent, manager, employee contractor or sub lessee from the leased area at the rates prescribed for that purpose. Clause 1 of the proviso to Rule 21 further provided that no royalty shall be charged from Nimbhadas of villages potters who manufacture upto one lakh bricks per year. It further provides that no mining lease shall be granted for more than once during any period of three years. Sub rule 2(vi) of the Notification prescribed a ceiling on the amount of royalty which was raised in 1981 and also provided that the holder of the Parwana granted under the Rules shall pay a royalty at 5 per cent of the rate specified in the Schedule. The validity of the Rule was considered in B.K. Trivedi & Sons and Ors. vs State of Gujarat and ors., ; as under the said rule the royalty payable as royalty was being treated as part of the consolidated fund of the State and used for other purposes by the Government. Clause 11 of the notification provided that "the holder of any mining lease or a other mineral concession granted under this rules shall be paid royalty at that rate, but no royalty would be charged on the minerals removed or occupied by him santed either by himself, manager agent, employee, contractor or contractor or by sub lessee. The State Government had framed the GujaratMinor Mineral Rules 1979 which provided for the determination of the rates of royalty. Rule 21 was substituted by another rule by the issue. The question whether a mining lease was in contravention of clause (b) of Article 304 could not be decided on the facts and circumstances of that case though it existed prior to the amendment, no restriction was imposed on the freedom of trade of the petitioners by the levy of royalty on the extracted mineral for more over once during a period of 3 years. Allowing the petitions, ^ HELD: (1) The levy in question is not arbitrary and has been imposed in an arbitrary manner. [414C] (2) The power exercised is legislative in character, that it does not mean that the said tax should be used only for development of mineral minerals and not for other pur pose sanctioned by law. If the executive or the administrative authority acts in an arbitrarily manner, its action would be bad in law and liable to be struck down by the courts but the possibility of abuse of power or arbi trary exercise of power cannot invalidate the statute con ferring the power or the power which has been conferred by it.

The appellant is the hereditary trustee of a temple. He was elected as a trustee by the Sengunatha Mudaliars of Manjakollai village. The temple was declared as an "exempted" temple under the Madras Act 1 of 1925. The case of the appellant was that the temple was the rounded two hundred years ago by the members of his community and since then the management of the temple and is affairs was always vested in the community of the Sangunathappan Ammal Community and no person other than the elected trustee had at any time the right of management and control of the deity. The appellant contended that the succession was "regulated by usage". Held, further, that the word "succession" in section 6(9) of the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951 would include even such cases. There need be no blood relationship between the deceased and his successor but the right should not depend upon the choice of any individual. In re: Hindu Women 's Right to Property Act, 1941, (1) 63 I.A. 448; applied. Article R.N. Sen vs The Commissioner of Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras, [1954] S.C.R. 469, distinguished. State of Madras vs Ramakrishna, ; , followed. State Darjee Bahadur vs Kamalabrata Mullick, A.I.R., 1954 S. C. 254, approved. State vs Ramakrishna; , relied on. Under section 6 (9) the appellant must be deemed to have been a hereditary trustee within the meaning of that section and not for life. The contention that the office of the appel lant is hereditary within the terms of section 6 was not well accepted. The word "subsequent" in relation to property and rights and interest in property generally implies "passing of an interest from one person to another", and when so construed that part of the definition would only apply where the ordinary rules of succession under the Hindu law were modified by usage and succession had to be determined in accordance with the modified rules. The words "su Budccession to this office" would include only such cases, was an impossible legal position.

The appellant was charged with murder of one person and the deceased was acquitted by the trial court. The High Court, after discussing the entire evidence, rejected the evidence of these eye witnesses, namely, PW 1, 2, 3 and 5 and described them as "a bunch of liar", "unashamed liars andensibleurers". The High court held that there had been a history of bitter feud spanning over nearly a decade between the first accused and his father on the one hand and the appellant jagirdar on the other. It was also observed that the High Court 'can place no reliance on the testimony of PW 4 in so far as he implicated the second accused and Tharnizasan in the case of murder of Viswanatham". Allowing the appeal by special leave, HELD: There is a mention about a pool of blood only where the dead body was found at No. 1 and there were also no blood stains on the bench where he was said to be sleeping. The fact that the witness has stated in the first information report that the deceased being only mentioning the name of accused Karunakaran as his assailant, this earlier version appears to be contradicted by the medical evidence. Besides, PW 4 has deliberately changed his own stand in Court when he deposed that he saw two other persons running ahead of legatean being chased by his two brothers and Ramaswamy. Another very serious departure from his earlier version is that while PW 4 had stated in The first information Report that the appellant was only mentioning that the name 'L159 ' is "chasing him from behind" in court he has completely given a go by to this statement and stated that Karunakaran was being chased with by PWs 1,2, 3. He did not at all refer to the deceased chasing him. If his statement in Court that he found PWs 1 2 and 3 chasing Karunakaran while running away after the assault is true, it is difficult to appreciate that he would not mention about this fact in the First Information Report. He admitted in the course of cross examination that the Sub Inspector asked him whether he had any witnesses and that he "did not tell about them due to excitement".

The respondents were partners in a firm of solicitors. They kept its accounts on cash basis and they maintained the accounts on such cash basis. For the assessment years 1950 51 to 1954 55 the Income tax Officer sought to tax these realisations but it was rejected by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeal holding that section 24B had no application and therefore the Income Tax Act had no applica tion to the case. On appeal by the Commissioner of Income tax, the High Court held that apart from section 24E the amounts were not taxable and that the section had no appli cation to this income received after the death of Amarchand and that it was capital receipt and not revenue receipt. The department appealed to this Court by way of special leave. Held: (i) In view of the provisions of section 24 B of the Income lncome tax Act, 1922, it could not be said that they were income which may be deemed by fiction to have been received by the deceased person. (ii) Section 24B did not authorise levy of tax on receipts by legal representatives of a deceased person in the years of assessment succeeding the year of account being the previous year in which such person died and therefore they were not liable to be taxed as income (1) 19 T.R. 10, M. Kamdar, vs Commissioner of income tax, Bombay City; , , re G. N. Kamakar, Shoudhurani and Co., Ltd. vs Commissioner Of Income tax , Calcutta, , re Sreemati Usharani Shoudh Udayarani Sh likehurani, , , referred to.

The petitioners, who were appointed directly by promotion or by transfer to posts reserved under the Andhra Pradesh Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence) Rules, 1959, challenged the Act and the proposed action as ultra vires the Constitution. The contentions raised before the High Court were: (i) That Article 16(3) of the Constitu tion which provides for equality of opportunity in matters relating to employment or appointment to any office under the State, is constitutionally valid; (ii) that the word 'State ' here was to be understood in the extended meaning given to it by the definition of that word article 12. The legislative power to create residential qualification for employment is thus exclusively conferred on Parliament; Parliament can make a law which prescribes. any requirement as to residence within the State or Union territory prior to appointment or appointment, to an office in that State orUnion territory prior thereto or appointment. (iii) It has already made a declaration that no person shall be disqualified for any office in the territory of India because of his residence in any particular part of India. The contention of the petitioners was that the State Legislature, while prescribing the requirement, may prescribe the requirements of residence in a particular part in passing the Constitution, has not dealt with such an objection; (iv) That the requirement might be also as to resided under the Union Territory or part of that State and, therefore, Parliament is supreme and can make any law on the subject as the Article says. (v) The words 'any requirement ' cannot be read to warrant something which could have been said more specifically. The word 'state ' here is to be construed in the wider sense of the ordinary meaning given by the expression in that article, whereas there may be no discrimination among other things on the ground of residence. Realising therefore, that sometimes local sentiments may have to be respected or sometimes an inroad from more advance States into less developed States may have had to be prevented and a residential qualification may, therefore have to he prescribed, the exception in clause (3) was made. Even so, that clause speaks of residence within State. The claim of Mr. J. Das seeking to put a very wide and liberal construction upon the words ' any requirement ' can be read into warrant something. which could not have been so more specifically; These words bear on the kind of residence or its duration rather than its location within the state. (vi) That cl. 3 confers an additional right on Parliament to make laws for the further implementing of the law made by Parliament is valid and not. The requirement cannot be treated as reasonable.

The appellant was charged with offences under section 52 of the Indian Post Office Act, 1898. He was tried and convicted for offence under sections 467 and 471 of the Penal Code and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a period of one year in each case. The High Court on appeal held that he had secreted the articles from the mere fact that they were found in the almirah which was said to have been in his exclusive possession. It could not be said that the five registered letters were in the exclusive possession of the appellant, and therefore, the search was illegal inasmuch as it was in contravention of section 342 Code of Criminal Procedure: Held, further, that the prosecution has failed to prove that these letters were recovered from the possession of an officer of the Post Office in being in his possession exclusively or jointly with his father. The mere fact of possession, according to the counsel, does not suffice, to show that the articles were 'in the exclusive Possession for an inordinate length of time. It is common experience that delivery of postal articles is now and again delayed for a considerable length of ly time may be through accident or through the negligence of the postal employees. It would be difficult to understand why the father, if he happened to get possession of articles from some source may not have kept them in the Near godowns of the office, would be committing theft but it has not been found that he committed any theft. The shortage which is, how and how, has occurred is, therefore, a speculative reason and must, therefore be left out of consideration.

The High Court held that the Nyaya Panchayats exercised judicial powers and acted, even if the Panchas failed to record evidence, they cannot be held guilty of contempt of court. In appeal by special leave the appellants contended: (i) That a person who had knowledge of the order must prove this fact beyond all reasonable doubt. If there is any doubt about the benefit ought to be given to the person charged with contempt of Court. If a person bona fide comes to the conclusion on the material placed before him that the source of information is not authentic he cannot be found guilty of criminal contempt of Courts for disobeying the order; and (ii) that in such matters those who assert that a person had knowledge could know of the existence of the Order must prove it beyond all reasonableness. Held:(i) The High court did not appreciate that the so called affidavit which was filed before the Pancha Tenants was in fact not an affidavit at all. The Special Leave Petitions were the petitionable to appeal under article 136 of the Constitution. (ii). Section 123(c) is a serious matter and a High Court should be chary of finding a judicial officer guilty of breach of court for disobey ing its orders unless there is unimpeachable evidence that the judicial officer had knowledge by virtue of an affidavit sworn to before a person authorised to administer oaths. Therefore, no contempt of this Court has been established because a Court is entitled not to act on an application which is not accompanied by an affidavit properly sworn to or a certified copy of the judgment and he urges that the Magistrate was not bound to do so and, if he bona fide does not in his discretion adjourn proceedings it cannot be said that he has committed contempt of any court. (iii) The action of theAST Panchas in not doing so is obviously not bona fide and 120 amounts to wilful disobedience of the High Court 's order.

The appellant was charged with murder of a deceased. He admitted his guilt but denied the other allegations for the prosecution. The courts below, relying on certain statements made by the appellant in his report dictated at the Police Station and considered those facts together with the motive and the evidence about the purchase of the sword sufficient to confirm the appellant 's conviction and sentence. The High Court also did not rely on this extrajudicial confession which was inadmissible in evidence as its contents amounted to a confession of the offence by the accused made to a police Officer and that the evidence relied upon by the High Court was insufficient to establish that the appellant had murdered Sheo Sahai. The appeal by special leave is against the judgment and order of the High court dismissing his appeal, confirming the conviction and sentences awarded to him. The main contention on behalf of the appellant is (i) that he purchased a cycle from the deceased; (ii) that there was a quarrel in a play of cards; (iii) that as the appellant was not present when thequarters related to them the fact which had taken place at night and by Bishram Singh, P.W. 3, who deposed that the Sub Inspector was not available when Ujagar Singh related to him the fact that he had purchased a sword day before the incident and deposited it stained with human blood immediately after the murder; (iv) that the extra judicial confession together with an circumstances relied on by the courts below were insufficient to justify the rejection of the statement of the accused about the appellant his confessing to him that he did not commit the murder of Sheo Sahai and thereby causing his death were admissible in evidence, Held, that the statements made in the report dictated by the SubInspector at the police station and considered these facts together along with the background to which the confession of Ka Singh was recorded) and rejected. In the circumstances of this case it is not necessary to rely on the admissions of the prosecution witnesses in the order to sustain a conviction for the offence under section 302, I.P.C., and the High evidence having been rightly accepted, the courts were justified in rejecting the statement made by them. (i)(a) The extra judicial confessions are not usually considered with favour but that does not mean that such a confession coming from a person who has no reason to state falsely and to whom it is made in circumstances which tend to support his statement should not be believed; (b) Though they are connected with the deceased, it cannot be said that the confession coming of a person as against a person when he had enmity, had committed the murder. There is no reason why the appellant would not make such a statement when the appellant himself proceeds to the Police station and hands over the blood stained sword. It is enough if having blurted out the truth to be proceeded to the police Station and report the matter there. It may be that having blought out the falsity to be proceed to the State and report about it, the matter should not have been considered. The confession came from a persons who had enmity with Sheo Sahai, the appellant did purchase a sword and delivering it stainedwith human blood. When the accused 's statement made it very likely that what he stated did happen was that there could not have appeared any improbability in Ujagar Singh 's presence in his field on account of the crops being not very high a which made them doubt the appellant "s confessing" to him, that he would not made such a declaration when the accused himself proceeds partly to the report.

The first respondent published a preliminary electoral roll on September 30, 1978 under Rule 4(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Munici pal Corporation (Preparation, Revision and Publication of Electoral Rollsand Selection of Councillors) Rules 1963. The candidates presented a petition in the year of October 19, 1978 requesting the Court to make an order quashing the electoral roll and the calendar of events issued for the purpose of the said election and directing the respondents not to notify the results of the election under Rule 46 of the Rules pending disposal of the writ petition. The petitioners submitted that their claims were rejected by the Deputy Collector without following the procedure prescribed for the preparation of the electoral rolls, and that as they did not produce any evidence in support of his claim, his application was dismissed. On December 30, 1980, the respondents filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court praying that a further direction to be issued to the respondents calling upon them to hold the election after preparing the electoral Roll afresh in accordance with the provisions of the Act and the Rules; and prayed for the issue of an interim order staying the poll which had been fixed to be held on December 31, 1978. On January 20, 1979, the High court dismissed the petition holding (i) that respondent No. 2, the Deputy collector had asked him to appear before him on October 30,1978 and that since he did not produced any evidence of his claims, his applications could have been disposed of on October 20, 1978; (ii) that none of the persons mentioned in Annexure P 7 preferred any claim before respondent No 's. 2 on October 15, 1978 and that he did so; (iii) that if they felt that the said notice suffered from any illegality, they could have brought it to the notice of the Collector immediately thereafter; and, therefore, the declaration of results of all the 44 successful candidates was liable to be quashed. On behalf of the respondents it was contended that (i ) though the petitioners were not prompt in moving the High Courts before the order was passed under Rule 6(3) of Rule 4 on October 25, 1978, they did never comply with Rule 4 (1); (ii). The High Court after hearing the parties dismissed the writ Petition holding (a) that the respondents were not entitled to any relief under Article 32; and (b) that they had approached the Deputy Commissioner, and therefore the writ application itself was presented on December 28, 1978 for challenging the validity of the elections. Allowing the appeals and dismissing the Writ Petition in part, ^ HELD: 1. The failure of the petitioners to comply with rule 4(3), as it stood on February 20,1979 that they never knew immediately after the publication of such notice that in the said notification a period of 20 days had been mentioned in its preamble as the period within which the claims and objections could be preferred and in paragraph 7 thereof it had been stated that any such claim or objection filed beyond the prescribed period was liable for rejection. [418 A C] 2.

The State of Bombay, was charged with failure to Me with the Registrar of Companies on or before 30 10 1967 the balance sheet and profit and loss account of the company as required under section 220(1) of the Indian , which is punishable under sub section (3) of that section. Admittedly no general body meeting had been held and, therefore, the balance sheets and profit & loss account had not been laid before a general body. The Full Bench in appeal by special leave granted to the State under article 136 of the Constitution and explained the position. Two questions arose for decision in this case: (1) Whether the failure to comply with section 131 of the Companies Act, 1913 or section 220 of the . was made punishable under section 134(4) of tho Companies Act ? (2) whether the failure of holding a general meeting and laying before it of the balance Sheet and profit loss account before that it may expose the person responsible to punishment under other provisions of the Act, it certainly does not make him liable under the provisions of section 134 (4) or section 221 of the and is an essential condition precedent to the requirement that copies of such documents so laid should be filed before the Registrar. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD : The company and its directors could not rely upon their failure to call the general body meetings as a defence to the prosecution. [416 D] The High Court was therefore right in holding that because section 26 provides that if no balance sheet is laid before the general Body, there can be no question of that balance sheet not being adopted nor comply with the requirements of the sub section(2) of section134 of the companies Act or section220 of the , as the case may be. [417 E] In the instant case, the holding of the annual general meeting, and the laying before the company of the share sheet and the profit and Loss Account is a sine qua non for filing of the copies thereof before the respondent Registrar. If no such balance sheet was laid before any general body, there could be no questions of that fail in prosecution under section134(4). [416 F G] It may also be that copies have been forwarded under sub sections (1), 20 and 21 of the Income Tax Act or sub section 2 of section 220. But since no general board meeting is held, the persons concerned cannot be said to have committed a default in complying with those provisions. [414 A B] The State of Madras vs Vulcan Industries Ltd., ; followed.

The respondent and 49 other persons were charged with various offences alleged to have been committed by them in the course of their raid as an armed gang on a certain factory known that the Jessop Factory at Dum Dum, and they were convicted and sentenced to varying terms of imprison ment by the Special Court to which the case was sent for trial by the Governor of West Bengal by a notification dated 26th January 1950. The State Government contended before the High Court (i) that section 5 (1) of the Act in so far as it enabled the State Govern ment to direct any particular case to be tried by a special court constituted under the West Bengal Special Courts Ordinance, 1949, offended article 14 Of the Constitution inasmuch as the classification was based on a reasonable classification of persons to whom or the offences in respect of which the procedure laid down in it was to apply, and (ii) that the classification must not be arbitrary but must be rational. Held, further, that inasmuch as section 5(1) was designed only for the trial by a Special Court of certain of fences or classes of cases and an appeal provided against such conviction would lie only with a recommendation that all offences which in its opinion require speedier trial should not be tried under any other law. Held further, also, that section 6 of the West Ben ch Code authorised the State Government to direct "cases" to be try by Special Court according to the special procedure provided by it for the speedi er trial of certain offences. The classification implied in this part of the sub section was valid if the State gov ernment classifies offences arbitrarily and not on any reasonable basis having a relation to the object of the legislation. Harries C. J., dissenting. A member of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes had been trying him at the trial for an offence under s.5 (1). Held also, further that section 4(1)(v) was valid since it did not necessarily require the conviction by the High court on any particular ground, and in fact it gave no directions to the State Legislature or Parliament (by an executive authority) directing "cases". A classification based on this part could be made only by a conse quned authority whose decision had been taken by the State but was concerned with the grouping of "offences" altogether. The entire section was not unconstitutional as it did. The discrimination being alleged against officials in carrying out the law, a question of intention might be material in ascertaining whether the officer acted mala fide or not (1), and consequently a conviction could not be sustained.

The appellant was appointed as a Lecturer in Radiology in a hospital which is attached to the Maulana Azad Medical College. He, inter alia, possesses the minimum educational qualification prescribed for teaching post. By a notification dated January 1, 1965, the initial appointments were notified. The essential pre condition for the inclusion of a post in the Central Health Service was that a medical qualification recognized under the Indian Medical Council should be prescribed for it. By the said notification the initial appointment was notified. On January 14, 1963 the appellant was called by the Banaras Hindu University for an interview on August 7, 1972 for the post of Professor of Radiotherapy but since the post was falling vacant in 1973, he did not appear for the interview. He filed a return reiterating the stand taken by the Government of India in the Health Ministry that the experience gained by the appellant as an Associate Professor from the Indira Gandhi Nehru Gandhi Gandhi University could not be taken into consideration for determining his eligibility for appointment as Professor or Radiology (ex officio) in the medical college inasmuch as he did neither possess at least five years ' teaching experience as Reader/Assistant Professor nor possessed at least 5 years teaching experience. He also contended that the appellant could not therefore be considered for appointment to the post as a Associate Professor, but was further integrated with the teaching under graduate and Post Graduate students as an Assistant Professor of Pathology (Ex officio) both by the University of Delhi as well as by the Ma Shalini Azad Medical college. The Government of Punjab in its letter dated January 17, 1976 informed the Principal that it was not possible to relieve the appellant of his duties or place his services on deputation with a lien on his post as Radiologist in the Irwin Hospital and provided it was denied that he was an Graduate Professor or Associate Professor in the Willing don Hospital or the Safdarjang Hospital and that the post could be filled up by direct recruitment only in the manner specified in the Second Schedule. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the aforesaid notification but the learned single Judge dismissed it as infructuous on January 9, 1979. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant: (i) that the appointment of the appellant to the posts of Assistant Professor and the post which was created more than two decades ago could not he taken into account for determining the question of his eligibility; and (ii) that since the appellant did not hold the post or of an Associate professor, he was not in direct line of and eligible for promotion to the Post of Associate Professor. Allowing the appeal ^ HELD: 1. The post of Assistant on which the appellant holds in the Higher Secondary School is a post belonging to Specialist Grade I which is equivalent to Supertime Grade II carrying a pay scale of Rs. 8(3) provides that 50% of the vacancies in Category 'B ' of the super time scale were to be filled by promotion through Departmental Promotion Committee of officers holding the Post in the senior scale who had rendered not less than six years of service in that scale and 20% of these vacancies were to he filled by direct recruit in the post.

The workmen of Orient Paper Mills Ltd., Brajrajnagar, are inter alia the workmen of a company in which the Company is also an inter alia engaged in manufacturing paper. In accordance with the provisions of the Cement Control Order, 1959 and any scheme made by the Company under the Act, the Company took into account two different items of dispute viz : (a) bonus for workmen between the Company and the Company, (b) dearness allowance payable to them on the basis of their wages in comparable industries in the region. The Tribunal referred the matter to it which was referred to the Tribunal for adjudication under section 10(1)(d) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, for adjudication by the Tribunal enumerating 30 different items Of dispute which included the minimum wages and dearness allowance, in addition to Rs. 95. On reference, the Tribunal held that there were no other concerns in the same line of business as the Company in the industry which could be compared with the company and that therefore, it would not be proper to compare the wage structure for those Paper Mills with that of the Company. In a petition under article 226 of the Constitution filed by the workmen challenging the award on various grounds including (a), that there was no geographical area or a geographical area in which such industry could be linked with the Company; and (b). there were only other industries in tho region where the minimum wage was fixed for the Price Index No. 441 prevailing at the time of the award taking 100 as the basic price Index for the year 1939 In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the workmen that the Tribunal committed an error inasmuch as in making the calculation the Tribunal only tried to neutralise about 36 per cent of the cost of living had been made variable with the Price Silicate instead of allowing neutralisation to the extent of at least 90%. It was also urged that two other reasons were taken by the company for fixing the minimum pay in the Company 's favour, namely (i) the Tribunal has not laid down the principle in French Motor Car Co. vs Workmen. [1963] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 839; and, (ii) the object of standardisation, by increasing the same wage structure at a certain percentage was to eliminate persons from getting higher wages. HELD : (i). The minimum wage fixed by the tribunal must be within the limits prescribed in the Act. But there is no absolute standard or vague classification. The principle laid down in French Car Co., 's Case (1) that where the dearness allowance forms a part of the consolidated wage fixed, there should be such linking so as to bring in continuous variation of the wages depending on the variation in the Price Umeshchandra Mafatlal vs M/s. British Paints Ltd. [1959] Supp 1 S. C.R., 866 referred to. (ii). The Tribunal was not correct in applying the principle laid by this Court in French car Co. case to fix the minimum ' wage in the company on the recommendations of this court in the case of French Motor Workers ' Case.

The business of the appellant was carried on by a firm which carried on the business as a result of a transfer by an instrument executed on February 7, 1948. The partnership deed provided that this firm carried on business in the manufacture and sale of cotton yarn and tobacco yarn and the branches were split up into two separate shops. The partners did not carry on their business at each other but continued to carry on one single partnership business. Under the provisions of the Income tax Act, 1918, which came into force on April 1, 1939, the business was carried out by two independent firms, the firm was to carry out and continue the existing partnership business under the name and style of 'Sait Nagjee Purushotham and Co., Bankers and Piece goods. The appellant claimed that it had transferred its business to a limited company with effect either from November 13, 1947 or February 13, 1948 by an agreement executed on January 7,1948. Held, that where the partnership was dissolved but the business continued in existence there being change in the constitution of the firm it did not cease to exist after the benefit of section 25(3). The finding that the business in soap and umbrella was different from the business of banking, piece goods and yarn and that the two partners constituted two separate firms did not amount to "discontinuance" of the business for the application of sub section (4) Of section 25. Accordingly, the Tribunal was right in holding that the appellant could claim the benefit mentioned in section 25 (4).

The plaintiff 's suit based on the provisions of section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1947, was contested by defendant 1, who by his application dated November 6, 1962 had made it clear that 'a partition had taken place between him and his two sons in December 1952 and December 1954 and that by a family arrangement dated March 31, 1955 he bad given directions for disposal of the share which was reserved by him for himself. The trial court rejected defendant 1 's case that the properties belonged to the joint family consisting of her husband 's wife, herself and their children, each having an equal share, the plaintiff 'sets 1/4th share therein. The defendant 1 filed first appeal No. 524 of 1966 in the Bombay High Court, while the plaintiff filed cross objections. By a judgment dated March 19, 1975 a Division Bench of the High Court dismissed defendant I 's appeal and allowed the plaintiff"s cross objection by holding that the suit properties belonged exclusively to the Joint Family and that there was no prior partition and that the plaintiff is entitled to a 7/24th share. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the Full Bench had given itself the view that the partition was not fully argued and was incorrectly decided, (ii) even assuming that two interpretations were reasonably possible the High Courts should have preferred another view; (iii) the remand of the case back to the trial court for taking a fresh decision in accordance with law after giving due and full effect to the fiction created by section 18A(9)(b). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The decisions on which the plaintiff relies are not erroneous. The view which the High. Court was taking is that the suits properties belong exclusively to ' joint Family and there was nothing in the instant case, by the application of the proviso to section 6.

Paragraph 12 thereof provided that "the age of retirement shall be 60 years" subject to the appointing authority at its discretion extend the age of superannuation to 60 years as provided therein, continued to apply; but all the transfer 200 red employees belonging to Class III and Class IV and the transferred employees insofar as the age Of retirement was concerned. In the case of the other employees who joined the service subsequent to 1st September, 1956, regulation 21 of the (Staff Regulations), 1960, which prescribed the age for retirement at 55 years subject to exemption from compulsory retirement vested in the Corporation and pending the appointment of the Corpora tor and which had been brought into force with effect from July 1, 1960 were suitably amended to bring it in conformity with the settlement. Regulation 19(2), however, provided that the appointing authori ty may extend ana tion at its pleasure the service of any employee of the Corpo ration belonging to the class I or Class II categories appointed to the service on or after 1st Septem ber, 1956 for one year at a time upto 60 years of age. Prior to January 1955 there were more than 200 insur ers carrying on life insurance business in India. As it came to the notice of the Government that the Indian Life Insur tors, with a few exceptions, had virtually controlled by few individuals who were utilising the funds of those companies to the detriment of the industry and had the policyholders, the Govern ment decided to nationalise the life insurance busi ness. Pursuant to the decision, the President of India promulgated the Life Assurance (Emergency Provisions) Ordinance, 1956 on January 19, 1956 providing for vesting of the management of the life Insurance business (which was called the controlled business under the Ordinance which was being carried on by any insurer in India on that day in the Central Government and providing for its management. After the passing of the said Act, the management was required to be in charge of the Management of the business for and on behalf of the Central Govern ment and pending its appointment of all the employees belonging lo Class I or class II to which those officers would have held the same on the appointed day if this Act had not been passed. However, prior to January, 1955 there was more than two insur bers carrying out life insurance policy business in the country. As a result of the setting up of the new scheme by the Ordinance the management became vested in and vested with the Central Govt. and pending appointments of the employees of the Corporation on or before 1st Decem ber 1956 were required to retire on completion of 58 years of service subject again to the power of the Govern tment to retire any such employee on completion Of 55 years of Ananda tion. By r. 19, the appointing au thority may at its option extend his service for one 6 year at an age upto 60 1/6 times the age age of 60 years. In order to avoid a conflict between cl.(c) and cl. (bb) of sub section (2) Of section 49 of the Act, it was contended that the discrimination made between the employees vis a vis those constituting them in two categories was not invalid since they belonged to two distinct categories of employees who were governed by different conditions of service as regards pay, perquisites, allowances, administrative powers etc.

The appellants wrote letters on 20 February 1975 to the President with copies to others/the District Bar Association, Bhiwani. The letter was signed by 15 members of the Bar belonging to the District Bar association Bhiwani and in that letter they brought to the notice of the President that Justice D.S. Tewatia of the Punjab and Haryana High Court visited the session division of Bhiwani, inspected the courts from 14 February 1975 onwards to 19 February 1975 and the meeting was to be held on 17 February 1975. In that letter also they said that the Judge met the members of Bar on 15 February 1975 in the Bar Room, Bhiwi. On 22 February 1975, Shri Virender Kumar accompanied by his two other friends participated in the Conference and gave an impression that he was not a Judge but a politician who had come to Bar room. When the members were taken to meet the learned Judge, they told him that the library of this Bar seems to be very poor. The appellants threatened the President at Bar that time then he said: "that the Advocate General is of the view that the letter does not bear out any foundation for an action for criminal contempt." All the five members of these Bar Association filed affidavits in this pattern. In the affidavit filed by the deponent, it was stated inter alia stating: "a) that the contents of the letter which he and others addressed to Shri Varender Kumar Single a member of the District bar Association Bhiwani have been reaffirmed and that the said letter does no interfere much less substantial ly with due course of justice or proper administration of law by the courts. (b) that there was no intention whatsoever on his part to scandalise the Hon 'ble Judge or this Court or to lower the authority or undermine the prestige of the learned judge or of the High Court or of any of these people in the administration of justice". The petition was contested by the appellants and it was contended that : (1) there was a clear allegation that the Judges accepted hospitality of some organisa tion. (2) that on facts, it is a conditional apology; (3) that even if there was contempt of court there was never any occasion for acceptance of apology. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The High Court proceeded on the basis that the allegations in the letter were not disputed and challenged. [254 B] 2. When an out of the Court 's notice referred to the letter of the appellant and said "on a perusal of the contents thereof a prima facie case contempt is made out. The question was whether there was any contempt, but if it was alleged by the writer the matter would have to be ascertained by the court on facts whether the Judge concerned did speak on the matters ascribed to him before the Court would take any action against the persons who would criticise the Judge 's speech. [255 A B] 3. It is not a part of the duty of a Judge nor is it a duty in discharge of office of a judge to go and address a meeting on political matters to redress grievances of the people. However, if the speech of any Judge is criticised and if it becomes a disputed question of fact as to whether any Judge did speak or not as is alleged by him the matter might have to he ascertained by it at the court 's instance. [256 F] 4. In a case where in view of this Hon ' Supreme Court, the action of the deponent in addressing the letter in question constituted for any reason contempt of Court, one would be more sorry than the deponent himself. Therefore, the Single Judge fell into the error of accepting the apology without finding that the appellants committed any contempt. [252 F G] 5. The judgment is set aside.

The petitioner company was a registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. It was the managing director of another company Messrs. Jute and Gunny Brokers Ltd. A reference had been made by the Central Government under the provisions of section 5(1) of the Act before 58 1st September 1948, of the case of Messrs. jute and Gunn Brokers ' to the Investigation Commission appointed under Act XXX of 1947. During the investigation of some other cases similarly referred to the Commission it was said to have been discovered that the petitioner company had made secret profits which it had not disclosed and thus evaded taxa tion. The Commission notified the petitioners that their cases had been referred for investigation and they were called upon to furnish certain material, as detailed in Annexure "B" of the petition. The petitioners case was that these sections of the Taxation on Income (Investigation Commission) Act, 1947, have become void from the date of the commencement of the Constitution by reason of article 14 Of the Constitution. Held, further, that under the provi sions of section 3 of the , it is not limited to any period and in so far as proceedings had been initiated against the petitioners under the procedure of section 34 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, they are deprived of the right of appeal. It is well settled that where a person has evaded payment of income tax on income, or he is not entitled to be present at those stages and take part in the enquiry but after the material is ready and placed before the Commission, it can be said that he has evaded the payment of Income Tax. Under section 8 of the impugned Act the findings of fact given by the Commission as to factum and extent of evasion are final and conclusive, and thus the persons against whom proceedings are taken under section 5 (4) are deprived ,of the rights of appeal, second appeal and revision conferred by sections 31, 32 and 33, of ' the Indian Incometax Act on assessees whose cases are dealt with under the manner provided for in the provisions Of section 34.

The Respondent is a company registered under section 26 of the Indian Companies Act 1913. The primary objects of the Federation as set out in its preamble is "regulation of hours of work, payment of wages, leave, holiday terms of service and other conditions of work of persons employed in shop, commercial establishment, establishments for public entertainment or amusement and other establishments". Section 2(5) defines "establishment" to mean any premises where goods are sold either by retail or wholesale or where services are rendered to customers, and includes an office, a semantics room, godown, warehouse or work place whether in the same premises or otherwise used in connection with such trade or business but does not include a shop or a factory registered under the , or protects in relation to or incidental or ancillary thereto. The Act imposes the duty of working hours. Payment of wages is an integral part of the definition of "business". The other objects of a company are that to promote Indian business, and to provide for arbitration in respect of disputes arising between individual traders and business concerns in the course of trade, industry or transport; and manufacture, finance and all other economic subjects and to encourage Indian banking. Shipping and insurance was also included in section 2(9) of the Act. The question is whether the activities of the 6 Federation carried on in these premises amounted to "work in connection" with or incidental to trade or profession within the latter part of a definition which, according to the Respondent, is a business or trade? Dismissing the appeal by certificate, HELD: (1) While the definition Of 'establishment ' includes a shop and commercial establishment it cannot take the "out of the protection afforded thereby. The mere fact that the expression "industry" in section II(21) was wide enough to include a 'shop ' and 'commercial establishment. [354D E] Management of The Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry vs Their Workmen, ; , referred to. (2) It is immaterial whether its activities bring its premises within the ambit of a "shop" or a " commercial establishment". [353C D] R. K. Mittal 's case, (supra). In the instant case, the activity of the Union was not "a trade or 'business because by the Memorandum of Association Articles of Association and other material placed before the Court, it was held that these activities of Federation were also in the nature of material services within the wider definition of 'industry" given in the Act, and no part thereof could be paid as dividend or otherwise to any member. The respondent assessee was a Hindu undivided family headed by one Sri Trivikram Narain Singh who was the original founder and owner of what is known as Ausanganj State in the district of Benaras. The village of Benares loaded with Jagir became payable by the Zamindars direct to the Government. By this arrangement the revenue or land collections of Jagir became available by the jagirdar from year to year by the grant of the pension, Babu Hat Narain Singh and his successors no longer remained the proprietors of the Parganas or the jagir and became entitled to merely a pension. The letter written by which the amount of pension was determined at Rs. 36,322/8 is dated July 7, 1837 and was from H. Elliot Esqr., the Secretary to Lt. Government, N.W.P. Allahabad to J. Thompson Esq. Lt. Governor of Government, therefore, held that it was a regular annual income of the assessee and did not fall within the category of agricultural income tax. The source of the salary was a liability undertaken by the Government for extinguishing the proprietary rights of the Jagirdar and when the immediate source of income was not land or rent collections from land, it is difficult to hold that the receipt of the respondent was agricultural income within the meaning of section 4(3)(viii) of the Act. The High Court held that from the language of the letter of July 7 18 37, it was manifest that the right which was conferred was a right to share of one fourth in the net land revenue collections after deducting costs of Tahsil establishment. On appeal by special leave: HELD: (1) In this case the source of 'of income is clearly the arrangement arrived at in 1837 which and therefore it is not agricultural income as defined in the Act, [705 G; 704 A] (2) The allowance was revenue income and not exempt from taxation as agricultural income. [706 C] State of Uttar Pradesh vs Kunwar Sri Trivendram Narain. Singh, ; , followed.

The State Transport Corporation by its proceedings dated April 30, 1984 granted three out of the 14 permits to the Karnataka State Tourism Development Corporation and two permits to private operators. The Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation, the Karnataka state Road Transport Undertaking and some other private operators have filed these appeals by special leave of this Court under Article 136 of the Constitution. In exercise of its powers under section 63(7) of the , the Central Government specified 50 as the number of 'All India Tourist Vehicle Permits ' which may be granted by the Karnataka ' State Transport Authority. This notification is challenged in these appeals filed by private operators who had filed these appeal by special Leave. The parties to these appeals raised common questions of law and may, therefore, be disposed of by a common judgment. Before this Court it was contended on behalf of some private operators that the State Transport Appellate Tribunal and the High Court were wrong in distinguishing them. On behalf of private operators contended that the view taken by the High Courts and the State High Court was correct and that the fourth sub clause of the proviso to Section 63(1) contravened article 14, and had to be struck down. On the other hand, it was urged that (i) the preference contemplated by the proviso should not have been granted to the private operators; and (ii) the word 'preference ' occurring in section 47(1 H), in the back ground of the provisions of Chapters IV and IV A of the Act, under the former of which the State transport Undertaking would have preference whereas under the latter the State, Transport Undertaking would had a monopoly. Disposing of these appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court 's decision is unexceptionable. While it was true that section 47 (1 H) does not expressly refer to 'other things being equal", it appears to be implicit in the provision that other things are equal. This rule is a rule of preference and not a rule or of exclusion. [1013C E] 2. The word 'Preference ' used in section 2(29 A ) means that the authority must have been in the car hire business for a period of 2 years with the help of cars of indigenous make or cars obtained from elsewhere and should have sufficient contacts with travel agencies hoteliers/ahematics, etc. and should be financially sound or that they should be owning and operating five vehicles as tourist taxies of either indigenous make ' or acquired from elsewhere regardless of the period in the vehicle hire business or that these should be ex Defence Service personnel, who satisfy certain prescribed conditions. It is not necessary that the department should have personal contactsies with travel agents in the tourist business or to own five tourist taxes. There is no question of eliminating private operators merely because the Undertaking applies for a stage carriage permit under Chapter IV. [ 1013G H] 3. The general scheme of the Karnataka Act in the matter of grant of permits for stage carriages and contract carriages appears to he that except in the case of a notified route or notified area, where under section 68 F(1), the permit has to be necessarily granted to tho State Transport Undertaking, in all other cases, the claims of all eligible applicants must be considered on merits. applying the rules of preference wherever the claims are approximately equal.
