The respondent purchased, by a registered instrument dated October 5, 1956, the business carried on by one Purushottam Raju under the name All India Trading Company. Purshottam Raju was the sole proprietor of the business and had been assessed to sales tax in respect of his turnover for the years 1948 49 and 1949 50. The respondent paid some amounts towards sales tax thus determined but there remained some arrears of sales tax i.e., Rs. 3836 4 0 for 1948 49, and Rs. 1218 1 9 for 1949 50 The Sales Tax authorities attempted to recover the arrears of tax from the respondent as the purchaser of the said business. The Commercial Tax Officer held that the respondent was not liable to pay the sales tax due from his predecessor in title, Purushottam Raju. This finding Was confirmed by the Board of Revenue. The High Court allowed the petition holding that Rule 21 A was ultra vires of the rule making power of the State Government under section 19(1)(c) and the respondent wag not liable. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (i) that under section 14(2)(C) of the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939, an express provision was inserted by which the transferee of the previous business was made liable for the arrears under the Act; (ii) that there was no contractual obligation between the transferor and the transferee on the one hand and the transferor on the other; and (iii) that in any event the respondent undertook to pay not only Sch. I liabilities but also other liabilities like sales tax imposed in regard to the business. HELD: The word 'assessment ' used in section 19 (2)(c ) does not include the power of recovering tax assessed from a person other than the assessee. It follows therefore that Rule. 21 A is beyond the rule made power of State Government either under section19(1) or section 19A(2).

The appellant entered service in the Gondal State. In 1927, he was suspended and at that time he was acting as Accountant at Rajkot Central Prison, and on March 7, 1954, he had committed certain acts of mis appropriation of food stuffs meant for prisoners maltreatment of prisoners and acceptance of illegal gratification from them, but on enquiry held by him, the police found that the appellant 's conduct amounted to denial of reasonable opportunity contemplated by article 311(2) of the Constitution. The appellant 'reprehensible action taken against him in respect of arrears of pay from April 1, 1954 to May 7, 1956. He filed a written statement contending that the departmental enquiry was vitiated as he had not been furnished with copies of the report of the Enquiry Officer, and that the Inspector General of Prisons had recorded before him and the tentative conclusions arrived at by the Enquiry officer were bound to influence him, and in depriving them of a copy of the same he was handicapped. The High Court held that the failure on the part of the competent authority to provide the appellant with a copy, of the enquiry report amounted to violation of article 311 (2) Of the Constitution, as according to it there was no duty to supply a copy thereof and had not prejudiced by the non supply of the copy of his report. Held, that though some elements of relationship existed between a public servant and Government servants, the liability to pay wages when it has been fixed arises out of a contract to pay salary, is not lacking even in England where a special relationship exists between the Crown and its public servants. In the present case, however, some elements were of relationship which arose between the appellant and Government were based on contract within the meaning of section 60 of the Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960, and the liability arising out of them was one of damages. The decree of the High Court decreeing payment of arrears was truly a liability in proceedings relating to a contract within section 60(2)(a) of that Act rather than under section 61.

The appellant was the predecessor in interest of the predecessors in interest. He granted a lease of 96 bighas out of his property to one Walji Hassan, by a deed exhibit C(1), and on November 23, 1900, it appears that Samanta bad surrendered his rights under the previous lease in favour of M. It is alleged that in 1932 there was a survey of the plaintiffs ' land and removal of coal therefrom were alleged to have taken place in or about the year 1932. The respondents denied the said allegation and stated that they threatened the appellant that the later portion of coal which belonged to them belonged to and was the property of the appellant. The appellants contended that the map translated into words indicates that the correct boundary should be a line drawn from the true meeting point of the four villages Narendra Lal Bahadur Bahadur Bahadur; that the demarcation of this plot was in accordance with the revenue plan prepared by the department of Mines and before that they had absolutely no knowledge or information whatsoever about it. Held, that the question is one of fact and the finding must be based on a preponderance of evidence. The burden of proof lies upon the party who comes to court to get a decision on the existence of certain facts which he asserts. In other words, he has to prove that he first learnt within three years of the suit that the property which he is seeking to recover was in the possession of the defendant. Further, it cannot be held that the onus is upon the plaintiff to prove his knowledge of the fact on a particular date for the said fact and that the burden of proving that he obtained the knowledge of his father Was within three year of the trial. Held further, that under section 101 of the Indian Evidence Act, the burden in the former sense is on the party whose comes to Court to get decision on existence of such facts which it asserts. Under section 101 all the onus in the latter sense is upon him who comesto court to prove ,a fact that he has the knowledgeof the said facts on a certain particular date, for instance, if he proves that he had the knowledge about the said information on a relevant date, he would be within his peculiar knowledge. Thus, section 101 does not make it obligatory on a Court in the later sense. Where a person has a right to sue within three six years from the date of his coming to know of a certain fact, it is for him to prove the necessary facts. Therefore, it was not open to the court to reconstruct the plan with reference to revenue records when the plan was self contained and drawn to scale.

The appellant, a saw mill carrying on business in Kozihkode in 824 the State of Kerala. One Sankaran, was in the employ of the appellant as a crosscutter and was working outside. He was caught hold by other workmen and taken outside. It was said that he came again a short time later at 4 p.m. and abused the same persons again. Later an enquiry under r. 18 (a) of the Standing Orders was held, but there was no evidence to prove what had actually happened. The Tribunal ordered reinstatement of Sankaran with full back wages. On appeal by special leave to this Court, HELD: (i) The Industrial court has the right to inquire into the causes that might have led to termination of service even under a rule like 18(a) and if it is satisfied that the action taken under such a rule was a colourable exercise of power and was not bona fide or was a result of victimisation or unfair labour practice. [826 B C] (ii) Where the termination of services is capricious, arbitrary or unnecessarily harsh on the part of the employer judged by normal standards of a reasonable man that may be cogent evidence of victimisation and unfair labour practices. These observations were approved by this Court in The Chartered Bank, Bombay vs The Chartered bank Employees ' Union, ; [830 A C] Parshotam Lal Dhingra vs Union of India, ; , followed. Even if the inquiry was not held by the appellant and action was taken under r., 18 (A) it is now well settled that an employer can defend the action under R. 18(b) by leading evidence before the Tribunal to show that there was in fact misconduct and therefore it cannot be said that the industrial court could inquire into causes that led to the termination.

A suit filed against the owners of a cinema theatre was decreed by the Trial Court. A second appeal was filed before the High Court which dismissed it on the ground that evidence in the earlier suit it was not even averred that the rights granted were in the nature of leasehold rights; and, as regards the agreement dated November 27, 1954 that "case" created a lease. The Revision Petition filed by the defendants against that order was dismissed. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) A consent decree cannot operate as res judicata because a consent decree is merely the record of a contract between the parties to a suit to which is superadded the seal of the court. [446B] (ii) An order of the trial court refusing to uphold an objection to certain question asked to a witness under examination does not operate as Res judicata because, a consent decrees are merely the records of a contracts between the par ties to a matter decided by any Court subordinate to such High Court and in which no appeal lies thereo if such subordinate court appears (a) to have exercised a jurisdiction not vested in it by law or to have failed to exercise a jurisdiction so vested, or (c) to has acted in the exercise of its jurisdiction illegally or with material irregularity. [441C E] Major section Khanna vs Brig. F. J. Dillon [1586] 1 Ch. 132 and Major section K. P. Kulkarni vs Brig F.J. Dullon ; followed. (iii) A proceeding may operate as a res judicata only if there is an adjudication by the Court: the terms of section II of the Code leave no scope for a contrary view. [442C] (iv) This Court observed in Major section S. Khanna vs Col. Brig. Pomas, AIR 1973 SC 990 that "the expression "case ' is not limited in its import to the entirety of the matter in dispute in an action".

[243C] 2. [368 B] Sanwat Singh vs State of Rajasthan, ; , Ramabhupala Reddy & Ors. vs The State of Mysore, A.I.R. 1971 S.C. 460; Rustam Hussain Khan & Anr.

% The appellant was the Chief Justice of a High Court. Both the Judges had become members and got elected as members of the Legislative Assembly. The Governor, after consultation with the Chief Election Commission, appointed the Judge by warrant under his hand and seal for committing the offences stated therein. On receipt of an address from the President the President nominated the Judge to be the competent authority to remove him from his office. By an order made on May 25, 1969, he was removed from his place while functioning as Chief Justice. The appellant challenged the said order before the High Court and the writ petition filed in this Court by him challenging the validity of the order of removal passed against him. He contended that the President had not been given the sole power or the exclusive power to remove a Judge either of the Supreme Court or of the High Courts from his Head Office, being the authority competent to remove the Judge of the , 'High Court 's office in order to enable that authority to grant sanction for prosecution of the Judge under the provisions of Section 6 (1)(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The President contended: 1. A Judge will be liable for committing criminal misconduct within the meaning of clause (e) of sub section (1) of Section 5 of the said Act if he has in his possession pecuniary resources or property disproportionate to his known sources of income. It was also urged that for the purpose of deciding the question of applicability of the Act to a person holding such an office, he will be immune from the prosecution not only under Section 5(1)(e) as is the present case, but also for the other offences under Clauses (a) to (d). The argument was that no sanction was required for prosecution for the appellant after his retirement when the need and feasibility of grant of sanction under Section 6 had ceased. It could not be accepted that the power to appoint a Judge can be exercised only in respect of offences under cls. (a), (b) and (e); 1. The power to punish a High court , if one may so describe it, is to be found only in Article 2 read with Article 124(4) and 5 of Article 124 of the Constitution. Since the order was made by the President, the learned Solicitor General did not place reliance on clauses (a). and (b). The question whether a Judge of a Supreme Court can be prosecuted for having committed the offence of criminal misconduct as referred to in clause (c) is, therefore, of considerable importance to decide the main question in this appeal. Further, for the purposes of clause(c) it was necessary to consider the feasibility of granting sanction under section 6 of the . The scheme of the 1973 Act was that a public servant who commits the offence, of criminalmis sion, as defined in Section 21 of the Indian Penal Code can be punished in accordance with subchand (2) of s.5 after investigation of the offence in the manner prescribed and with the previous sanction of the competent author ity obtained under section6 of the] Act, in a trial conducted according to the prescribed procedure. The grant of previous sanction under s.6 being a condition precedent for the prosecution of a public serv ant covered by the Act, it must follow that the holder of an office who may be a public servants according to "the wide definition of the expression in the . Act but whose category for the grant of ' sanction for pro duction of offences is not envisaged by section 6 (i)(c). The President could be the proper authority under clause (b), to remove such a Judge as required by Section 6(1)4 and to release him from office at any time, if he was in possession or had, at any moment during his tenure in office, been in posses sion for which the public servant can satisfactorily account.

The appellants, a partnership firm, was made an application by the members of Tata Engineering Works Limited for adjudication under section 10(1) (d), industrial Disputes Act. After the award was made, an application was made by the Union stating: "In view of the increase that is being allowed in the basic pay I do not propose to revise the existing wage scale of Rs. 150/ to each draughtsman and Rs. 100/ to all other workmen in their basic pay. On the same date, the Tribunal disposed of the application by following order: "There can be no doubt that a flat increase of Rs 150/ will be allowed to each craftmen and Rs 100/ . I therefore have to be treated as equivalent to the basic salary of each employee. [177A B] State Government 's order required the Tribunal to revise each of the existing scheme of Dearness Allowance. The fitment has also to be done only after the flat increase is added to the present basic salary, and that the order dated December 22, 1978 of the Tribunal also does not reveal that there was any opposition by the company to the application for correcting the award so as to bring out what was intended. The omission of the words to each employee first after the figure Rs.150/ and again after the figures Rs.100/ was clearly an accidental slip or omission which the Tribunal was entitled to correct. [180C D] State Govt. 's Orders dated December 15, 1978, of the Industrial Disputes (Bombay) Rules 1957, which is as follows: "A Board, Court, Labour Court, Tribunal or Arbitrator may at any time, suo moto or on an application made by any of the parties concerned may correct any clerical mistake or error arising from an accidental mistake or omission in any proceedings, report, award or proceeding as the case may be, decision".

The respondents, an award had been made by an Industrial Tribunal fixing the pay of the employees at Rs. 2/2/ per day and in pursuance of the said award, the management of the appellant had entered into an agreement with the res pondents that effect would be given to the wage structure prescribed by the award. This agreement was subsequently published in Bihar Gazette as a part of the award and thereupon the management had entered upon an agreement for paying the employees wages at Rs 2/ per month and that led to the present claim made by the respond ent Nos. 1 & 2 under section 15 of the . The respondents contended before the payment of wages authority that the refusal of the appel lant to pay to them wages at the rate awarded in substance amounted to an illegal deduction from their wages, and that they asked for an order from the Authority directing the appellant to pay the said prescribed wages. The appellant raised two pleas against the resolu tents ' claim. The Authority rejected these pleas and held that section 15 was applicable to the case because the rates of wages fixed by the Award did not fall within the definition of wages prescribed by section 2(vi) and as such it had rejected the appellants ' contention that the applications made by them were incompetent under section15 of the Act before the Patna High Court by filing a petition under article 226 of the Constitution. The appeal was however dismissed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) By the terms of the contract between the parties the appellant paid its employees only As. /10 per day, and therefore led to, the present suit claim made. Therefore, even under the unamended definition of Wages, rates of remuneration prescribed by an award could not be included. [419 D] (ii) The basic assumption made by section 15 that wages payable under any award or settlement between the respondent employer and his employees make it reasonable to think that even though the period of operation of the same award and statutory period for which it remained binding on the parties may elapse in respect of both of which special provisions had been mad applied under sections 23 and 29 respectively the new contract would continue to govern the relations between the ac tors till it is replaced by another contract. This being so, it was difficult to accede to the argument that the wages prescribed were wages under section 2 (vi) of the , before it was amended.

The appellant was a Sub Divisional Officer in the Public Works Department, Pepsu. He was charge sheeted under section 409 of the Indian Penal Code for forging the thumb impression of one Parma, and under section 408 he was acquitted by the trial Magistrate but convicted him both under section 465 and section 409 I.P.C. The High Court held that the charge under section 477 A required sanction as the official capacity was involved in the very act complained of as amounting to a crime; but after the disposal of the appeal by the High Court, it was discovered that there was no order sanctioning the prosecution and that the Chief Secretary had committed a mistake in sending up the communication. The appellant contended before this court that the sanction under section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure for his prosecution was necessary for prosecuting the appellant under section 407(1). He relied on the decisions in Shreekantiah Ram Singh vs Emperor, [1948] L.R 75 I.A. 185 and R. W. Mathams V. State of West Bengal, (1950) L.L.R. 75 I A. 180; distinguished. Held further that sanction under Section 197(i) of Cr. P.C., for the prosecution was required as required by section 197 (1) Cr. The charge against the appellant did not fall within the scope of his duties and could be justified by him as done by virtue of his office. To claim to have paid the amount to Parma a token money as a public servant and to take his signature or thumb impression in acknowledgment thereof, the accused did not claim to had spent the amount in course of his official duties. The fact that he received a sum of Rs 51 alleged to have been misappropriated would not make out any offence under section 406 I. P .C., but on the facts no sanction was required for a prosecution under that section and it could not be said that there were no circumstances which made him guilty of an act amounting to criminal misappropriation or forgery. Hori Ram Singh v Emperor, (1948) L L. R 75 I J. A 180 applied.

Section 6 of the Indian Income tax Act ( Travancore Act, 1947) was amended by adding a proviso in section 14(2) which provided that "where any assessee sustains a loss of profits or gains in any year under any of the heads mentioned in section 9(1) he shall be entitled to have the amount of loss set off against this income, profits or gain in British India or in an Indian State and exempt from tax under the said provisions ". The proviso to the section provided for assessment of income tax in respect of the total income of the previous year if such loss was a loss on which no deduction could be made. Under section 24(1), the assessee was entitled to deduct the losses incurred outside Travancore State from the profits accruing and arising in that State, disallowing a deduction of the losses in British country and in States other than Travancore State against profits made in Travancore State: Held, per section 6 (a) of the income tax Act and under the Travancore Act (1 Of 1918), as amended by the Indian Incometax (Amendment) Act (XXIII of 1941) by which another clause (c) was added in the proviso to that section, " business carried on in British ; India or business in anIndian State" within the meaning Of section 6 of Act, were independent provisions and that, consequently (1) the loss under one head of profits could not be set off under another head, the taxability of income arising from each head being separate. The proviso was therefore to be read as providing something by way of an addendum or dealing with a subject which was foreign to the main enactment. Arunachalam Chettiar vs Commissioner of Income Tax, Madras (1932) L.R. 233 and Narayanaswami Chettiar vs Assistant Commissioner of Sales tax, [1959] Supp. 2 S.C.R) followed.

An employee of the appellant company raised a dispute regarding his retirement age. The workmen claimed that no workman should be retired from service before he bad completed 60 years of age. This dispute was referred to the Industrial Tribunal, Maharashtra. Before the Tribunal the Company resisted the workmen 's claim, but submitted that it was agreeable to introduce for its Bombay employees provisions similar to those which had been introduced by agreement for Calcutta employees retirement at the age of 58 subject to the employee passing a medical examination on reaching the age Of 55. The Tribunal found that in all these awards there was no dispute as regards the age and fixed hours of work and other similar matters industrial tribunals attach much weight to what has been done in other industrial concerns in the neighbourhood and in recent times whether by agreement or by adjudication, the classification of those cases could be made and decided on industry cum region basis. On appeal, there was a further finding that in some of these awards the age was not fixed at 60 or more. The Tribunals however did not agree with this view. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the workmen that the trend in Bombay region had been to fix the retirement age at 60 years and that there was change in the terms and conditions of service of those companies which were introduced by agreements for Calcutta III employees retirement, at the time when they raised a grievance, and that in any case, changing the terms, conditions of Service in regard to the age on retirement at 60 would not make the factory at 58, and hence the alteration in the award was bad. The question for decision in the present appeal was whether there was an error apparent on the face of the record. Held:(i) The Tribunals were ordinarily prepared to fix a date of retirement at a time when each workman had attained 60 or at the most there is a general agree ment that the age should be fixed at sixty. Such circumstances are not uncommon and varied with compared to those in other industries. Dunzlop Rubber Co. Ltd., vs The Workmen, ; and Dunzolop Rubber Company Limited vs Their Workmen, , followed. (ii)It was apparent from these decisions of this Court that the Tribunal went wrong in making those pronouncements. (iii)the approach adopted by it in dealing with this aspect of the problem was not very commendable. For finding out the recent trends in Bombay Region in which the decision was expressed was erroneous on the whole unsound. If the Tribunal had erred in making such those pronouncements, it would be the first to admit such mistakes and if it had failed to notice these infirmities, a point about it, namely, the decisions of the Supreme Court, however, remained. industrial adjudication has to pay special attention to the prevailing practice in the industrial region concerned. If in any particular region employee have been successful in their claim for fixing the age at 55 or 58, are special to them and do not show any recent trend in the matter. In spite of these infirmities this document was exhibit Cl. 3 of the Report of the Norms Committee, which came into force on October 1, 1959, and a notice had also to be taken in this connection of the report of the Standards Committee in which it was stated that in 25 of those concerns the clerical and subordinate staff were not organised into trade unions, There was thus good ground for thinking that the. reason why these concerns have kept the ageof retirement at 55 would be no justification. [445 C E] DunzIy Wordlop rubber Co., Ltd. vs Workmen, and Dunwnath Rubber Co., but in spite of this infirmity that had been recorded in the case, the Tribunal was unable to notice any slowing down of this trend.

The first respondent who was at that time Minister of Finance in the Government of India, and was engaged as an Inspector by the Company Law Board was called upon to submit his report under section 237(b) of the and (2) that the Chairman may distribute the business of the company among himself and the other members or some of them specified in sub cls. The appellants who were charged with offences under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced them to five years ' rigorous imprisonment, were convicted for dacoity. On appeal by special leave it was contended that sections 41 1 722 of the Code of Criminal Procedure had not been stated by law and therefore it was necessary always to start with the lesser presumption and draw the higher presumption only when there is some other evidence to show the complicity of the persons in the crime itself. HELD : The conviction was correct in all the circumstances of the case. As regards the sentence, the offence no doubt was serious but no injury beyond one appears to have been caused. Therefore, a sentence of three years ' imprisonment will meet the ends of justice in this case. [723 B C] In some cases there may be other elements which may point to the way as to how the presumption may be drawn. They need not be stated here for they differ from case to case to cases.[723 H; 723 A] The time gap in some cases is about 19 days and even then it is not more than five days. In two cases only a time gap is about 18 days. Even then there would be a considerable delay of more than six months and in some others it is unnecessary to have disposed of the property to these appellants Or to have left the goods in their custody till such time as the original offenders could take them away.] [727 D E] In the present case, the goods stolen were a large quantity of cloth taken for sale to the market. These goods were not sold and were being taken back to the dealers by the cartmen.) A large number of persons said to be 20 in number pelted stones at the cart men and looted the property. Immediately afterwards a number of searches were made, and the goods were found with various persons who were prosecuted as offenders and they had been presumed to be involved in the dacoity itself. It may be 723 impossible to think that these 20 persons were merely receivers of stolen property from some other 20 persons who might be the dacoits. There was therefore no question of presumption.

In Miscellaneous Writ Petition, the petitioners have challenged the provisions of section 5 of the (12 of 1919) (hereinafter called 'the Act). It was contended that though the Act is a Central enactment it is possible of unjust and unjustified discriminatory im plation as it is left to each State Government to determine what substance they would include as poison and regulated, and the decision in one State to include the substance as poison is not automatically made applicable to the other States. The object of the enactment was to regulate the posses sion for sale and sale of the same. In exercise of this power by the Notification No. F 10/44/72 fin. (G) dated 7.8.1973, the Lt. Governor amended the Delhi Poisons Rules, 1926 as a result thereof, amending the Delhi Subordinate Rules, by including to the list of substances included in the Rules as "Poisons" "the substance commonly known as 'thinner ' containing spirit and other soluble material such as shellac in which the percentage of such solu ble material did not exceed 30% as poison. The petitioners contended that although the Act was a Central Act it is ordinarily possible of harsh and unjustified discrimina tion as it was left to every State Government, to specify what substance them would include. It was further submitted that the restrictions imposed on possession for sale was not reasonable restrictions. The respondents contend ing in their counter statement that the Act as well as the 1982 Act were regulatory the petitioners contended before the authorities that in substance manufactured by them did not come within Rule 2(x)(2) and there were some correspondence in this regard, when the competent authority held that the substance manufactured was manufacturing only those thinners which contain only liquid substances like as ecotone, ethyl acetate SDS etc. and was not all solubles. The respondent contended that in essence manufactured by the petitioners did not came within Rule II(2). Allowing the writ petition this Court HELD: 1.1 The provisions of neither section 2 nor 5 nor the impugned notification are hit by any consti tutional limitation. [227H] 1.2 The provisions in both the Acts which show that a substance known as "thinerner" as it taken is or mixing with some other substances are taken as intoxicating spirit endangering the life. [229B C] 2.3 Section 4 of the Act expressly sets out certain guidelines when the State can notify a substance as confession. It states that the State Government may by rule regulate the possession of any specified poison in any local area in which it the use of such poison for the purpose of committing murder or mischief by poisoning cattle appears to it be of such frequent occurrence as to render restriction on the possis tion thereof desirable. Any substance which is used for purposes mentioned therein can definitely be declared as poison for tho entire country. The notification and its application to any area would depend on the necessity to declare the substance, as poisoning on the particular facts and situation prevailing in that area and the need to regu late the possession and sale in that areas. No question of discrimination can arise in such circumstances.

The appellant firm carried on business in drugs, chemicals, mercury camphor and art silk yam and as many as seven partners were admitted to the benefits of the partnership. The firm had dealings for several years with a firm known as "Bhojaji Sobhachand", carrying on business at Bombay as importers of yam & also as agents and adathias. The appellant firm was given dividends, but in appeal the amount was allowed in the return of income for the assessment year 1952 53 which included interest of Rs. 2,68,385 written off as irrecoverable. The Income tax Appellate Tribunal confirmed this order. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the loans made by the assessee were not loan '; and (2) the debt or any part thereof was in respect of loans in the ordinary course of money lending business, but a debt representing loss sustained in the other business. HELD: The question should have been referred to the High Court for its opinion. [422 D] (a) (b). It gives no reasons in support of the conclusions reached by the Tribunal that the sum in question was not one incurred in the course of the assessee 's business as Chemists and Druggists nor in respect thereof. [414 D E] (d) The tribunal has found in the documents produced by the Department that the sums in question were not loans made to the assessee. These findings are supported by the evidence on record.

On this ground alone, the Special leave Petitions are liable to he rejected.

The Tribunal held that there was no valid gift on the date of entry, then it could not be said that subsequently when the money was transferred by further entries in the same books, it resulted in a valid gift. All these officers are members of theOrissa Judicial Service, within the meaning of article 236(b) of the Constitution. Out of these, the district and district sessions judges were discharging purely judicial functions. In view of article 229 of the constitution. the power to appoint the Registrar is exclusively that of the Chief Justice, neither the High Court as such nor the Governor has any hand in his appointment. The High Court therefore directed the following transfers: (a) Shri B.K. Patro, Shri K. Bose and Shri P.C. Dey shall continue in the posts they were holding. (b) Shri T. Misra to continue in that post for an unduly long time. Section 15(1)(a) of the Punjab Pre emption Act, 1913 as it originally stood, underwent substantial changes in 1960 and as a result, section 15(2)(b) was amended. Section 15 provided for pre emption, in the case of sale of a share out of joint land or property and to which she has succeeded through her father or brother. By amendment of 1960 section 15 provided that where the sale is by a female of land or l earning land revenue or house within the vendor 's brothers or sisters ' sons of the vendor or vendors, then in order of succession, the right of pre emptment shall vest: (i) if the sale was by such female, in her brother or sister 's son 's sons of his vendor, or through her son in case the son has inherited the land or the property sold from his lather, the rights of sub emption shall vest; (ii) if for any reason, who are agnates, in order, of succession and thirdly, in persons not included under first or second above, in Order of succession who but for such sale would be entitled to inherit the proper neces sary land in the event of his or their decease, in that case, he would be entitle ed to inherit, the properly in the events of his/her death, to inherit and dispose of property under Article 19(1) (f), the same re striction was held to be valid when tested on the touchstone of Articles 14 & 15 of the Consti tution. The appellant contended that he fell within the expression other co sharers ' in clause 'Fourthly ' of section 15 (1)(b); and had not been sold jointly by all the co shar er. Disposing of the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. In the instant case, it was clear that the legislature desired to confer the right on specified family members of the lintee or vendors in the first three clauses of section15(1). [125E] 2. The object of the Legislature 's decision in Attam Prakash 's case was to deny the right to pre em enption conferred on specified class family members not specifically mentioned the preceding clauses, but only to cover all the remaining co sharer co shar es not specifically mentions the preceding clause. It will be noticed that priority for the exercise of the right owes statutorily fixed and even in the cases of those falling within the same class, the exercise has been regulated by the use of the expression, 'in order of inheritance; and thirdly in the co scri ch sharers, if any, who were agnts, in orders of succession. [125A B] 3.1 The object was that while co sharenors were entitled to preempt, the confer ment of that right on certain kinsfolk based on the rule of consanguinity being a relic of the feudal past could not be tolerated. This would clearly be discriminatory. [126C D] 3:2 The object and purpose of the legislation was to deprive co shar ers of their rights of previ tution conferred on them by that provision. It is difficult to hold that this Court intended to deny these two kins from the scope of clause fourthly of section 20(1), even if they happen to be co sharors.

With the death of respondent No. 2, an unregistered one, filed a suit for title and injunction. The petitioner had claimed that his three daughters were minors and their mother executed a Trust deed, bearing terms which they had accepted and all the parties have entered into a compromise with them whereunder the plaintiff was directed to pay Rs. 1 lakh from the date of the sale deeds. Respondent No. 3 in SLP(C) No. 542 of 1984 contended that the said alienations were valid and binding. The trial court decreed the suit on the ground that the defendants had not been paid Rs.1 lakh as stipulated and he had no intention to accept the compromise. In a second appeal, the High Court held that once the Court was satisfied that there was a compromise it was for the Court to record the same and no option lay before the court to act otherwise. Dismissing the special leave petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The alienation deeds are subsequent to 21.8.1987. In fact if the compromise is valid and lawful, the same has to be acted upon. There would be no order for costs. [540 A B] 1.2 If the compromise deed contains terms which were signed by the parties, the second respondent had disputed the fact of payment and had, in the meantime alienated about 81 acres of property which constitutes the subject matter of dispute to third parties. The alienees have admittedly been in possession of the property from the year of the sales which is more than three years old by now. Moreover, if the settlement deed is valid, and binding the alienor respondent No 2 had no interest in the property prior to 21st August 1987. [541 D F] 1:3 The alienee has made an attempt to hold out that there were agreements for sale prior to the compromise, for which there is no acceptable evidence. It was not done by the alienees. He sought to rely on certain decisions which on being referred to were found to be totally inapplicable to the facts of the case. On the other hand, we find that a similar question arose before the Orissa High Court in the case of Bhoja Govinda Maikap & Anr. vs Janaki Dei & Ors., AIR (1980) Ori. 108 wherein the power of the court under Order 23, rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the face of an objection of one of the parties to the compromised compromise was considered.

The respondent workmen, who were workers of the appellant company, felt aggrieved by virtue of a first proviso to section 49 of the , and contended that the benefit under the scheme of the Act was much less than the normal earnings of an employee and was not beneficial to the workmen. The Company also pleaded that there was no practice of giving any such sick leave in the industries in Baroda or in the State of Gujarat, that, therefore, it would create an absurd position inasmuch as a worker would receive more wages by remaining absent than on duty; and that under section 99 of the . It was also contended that, if the relief of sickness benefit was granted, it could not be construed to be adequate for, it works out to about half the average wage of a workman and even that amount was not admissible for the first two days of sickness except in the case of a period of maternity leave following. at an interval of not more than 15 days, the spell of sickness for which the sickness benefit Was last paid; and the workmen were entitled to 7 days sick leave with wages on full emoluments for a period Of 7 days when he was certified as a competent medical practitioner under section 55(b). The Tribunal rejected the contention on behalf of the workmen that the workmen did not deserve anything more than sickness benefit for the two days also, and that the amendment was allowed in respect of sick leave without pay. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf Of the appel lants that even though the Act which was applicable to the workers of dispo urities of sick Leave applied to the industry from December 14, 1969, and they were quite adequate, the Tribunal committed an error of law in granting to their demand for sickness leave. In this connection it was further contended that section 99 gave wide powers to the Employees ' State Insurance Corpora tion to enhance the benefit and that it was not bound by the provi sions of the scheme to allow sick leave to its workmen in the region; and since the benefit of sick, was lost when the Act being made applicable to a region from December 15, 1969. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.(i) The Tribunal has examined this aspect of the controversy also as also the question whether the benefits admissible under the Act could apply to the company or not. [83B] 1(ii). Section 61 of the is not in fact a bar to the demand of the workman for sick leave. The Act does not, therefore provide for any leave to the workman on the ground of sickness. It provides that when a person is entitled to any of the benefits provided by the Act he shall not be enti tled to receive any similar benefit admissible under other enactment. [86H; 87A] 2.(i). The appellant company was prevented from earning the normal daily wages during the period of his illness and there was nothing more than sick sickness benefit, for it could only be taken away under the mistaken impression that it had been adequately replaced by the new provisions on the coming into force of the Provident Fund Act. [87C D] 2(ii) It is not necessary in the circum stances of the case to award the benefit that the workman would get under this Act for it was taken away by the Tribunal with reference to the reports of the National Commission of Labour, 1969 and the norms Committee of Gujarat State which go to show that the benefits cannot b.e said to be proper as would deny him the bene fit of sick leaves on full pay for a calculated period of 7 days since he was neither able nor justified on that basis. [88D] 3(iii) Section 19 provides for periodical payment to an insured worker in case of sickness if certified by a duly appointed medical practitioner. It does not deal with all aspects of the demand for sick Leave; but it has been contended by the appellant companies that the scheme did not cover all contingencies of sickness and in any event, the first one waiting days were not covered.

The appellant was detained by an order of detention passed against him under section 3(1) (c) of the , as he had held a standing of about thirty years. He was in the Indian Air Force as an emergency Commissioned Officer between 1943 to 1948 and thereafter there on extension for another four years until he attained the age of 55. The detention order was challenged by the appellant on the ground that no particulars of the grounds could be furnished. Held, that when one who attempted to make a representation against the order under which he is detained, does not appear to have felt that the grounds furnished were so vague as to hamper him in his right to make an appropriate representation and to convey to it a request for obtaining the requisite particulars from the State under section 10 of the Act for their own knowledge and consideration. The words "the powers" in article 22 (5) are wide enough to include those which the authority considers to be against public interest to disclose". A right to call for particulars has been recognised in the case in the State of Bombay vs Atma Ram Sridhar Vaidya, ; , 185; Atma Ram sridhar Vaidyanya vs State of Maharashtra, [1955] 2 S.C.R. 1, referred to. The failure to furnish particulars and duty to consider whether the disclosure of any facts involved therein is against public interests cannot be said to have hampered his constitutional right of representation and an obligation to communicate cannot be implied in these circumstances. In the present case there was no merit in that contention. The order was therefore, mala fide.

" The respondent had attempted to identify himself by impersonating and giving false identity as "Mr. & Mrs. Prakash but he was refused. 's explanation was called for by the Central Government on April 9, 1959. On April 9. 1959, an order was passed removing the respondent from service under R. 14 of the Army Rules 1954. The respondent challenged his removal before the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution and the High court quashed the order. The appellant was a Panchayat as defined in the Bombay Village Panchayats Act, 1946. The Standing Committee appointed by the State Government under section 176(2)(xi) of the Act held that octroi duty shall be imposed on all the goods coming into the Panchayat limits for consumption, use or sale therein and at such rates as may be decided by them but not below the minimum and not exceeding the maximum rate specified in columns 2 and 3. The appellant challenged the validity of the levy contending that r. 5 of the Rules authorised the levy of octroi duty on all goods coming within its local limits as per the Schedule I item 1 to the Act and Rule 5 was ultra vires the Panchayat 's power to impose tax or fee imposed in accordance with law, and that, at any rate, the levy was good after the octroi limits were fixed on January 14, 1964, and whereas r. 7 provided that "the procedure prescribed in rr.3 and 4 should be followed before the Octroi duty can start being levied under the Act but it enjoins that the procedure prescribed therein shall be followed." The appellant contended (1) that r, 5 of Maharashtra Village Panchayats and Fees Rules was intra vires the Act inasmuch as it gave finality to the resolution passed by the Panchayat Samiti; and (2) that the approval of the octroi area on January 1, 1964 related back and therefore the levy could not be challenged. HELD: The Standing committee inspected the premises of the Company but in their order they have given very scanty facts they do not say whether the tea was crushed, processed or treated chemically to convert it into a marketable commodity. Since r. 3 merely prescribed that what the Panchayat does is to consider objections and suggestions, it would be seen that under r.3 what the panchayat does is is to decide whether the proposal about the tax selected by it for levy, but also the rules relating to that tax which must mean the action taken under the law and the rules.

An industrial dispute arose between the appellant No. 1 and its manager H. M. Khan who was accused No. 5. The conciliation proceedings were held and it ended in an order of dismissal by the Special Magistrate. On the question whether the conciliation proceedings could be said to be pending when Louis Pereira was dismissed, Held (per curiam) that section 12(6) of the , clearly indicates that the report should be made and the proceedings closed within a fortnight and if proceedings were not set closed but were carried on, as they were in the present case, or if the Conciliation Officer did not make his report within 14 days he may be guilty of a breach of duty but in law the proceedings do not automatically come to an end after 14 days but only terminate as provided in section 20(2)(b) which provides that where no settlement is arrived at when a memorandum of the settlement is signed by the par ties to the dispute, the effect would be to have been to have the expiry of 14 days. In other words, section 12 (6) contemplates the submission of the report by the Conciliation officer within 14 minutes but that does not affect the application of section 20 (2)(a). The provisions of section 12 of the Act are applicable to all conciliation proceedings whether in regard to utility services or otherwise. All conciliation proceedings under this sub section shall be deemed to have concluded in the case where no Settlement is arrived reached, when the report of the Conciliation Authority is received by the appropriate Government. The proceedings therefore do not end when the complaint under section 12 was made by the Pr. 15th January, 1952, and the termination would depend on how soon a report is received, by the Central Government or when the reference is made to a court Labour Court, Tribunal or National Tribunal under section 10 during the pendency of conciliation proceedings.

The petitioner 's activities were prejudicial to the maintenance of public order. The amount of detention was also challenged by him in a writ petition but this Court dismissed it without speaking order and also without any speaking order on his representation. Allowing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The Preventive Detention Act provides for preventive detention as contemplated by the various provisions of the different statutes dealing with preventive detention and should be used with great deal of circumspection. There must be awareness of the facts necessitating preventive custody of a person for social defence. If a man is in custody and there is no imminent possibility of his being released, the power of preventive detention should not be exercised. In the instant case when the actual order of detention had been served upon the detenu, the detenu was in jail. There is no indication that this factor or the question that the said detenu might be released or that there was such a possibility of release, was taken into consideration by the detaining authority properly and seriously before the service of the order. A bald statement has merely an ipso dixit of the officer. If there were cogent materials for thinking that the detenu might he released then these should have been made apparent. Eternal vigilance on the part of the authority charged with both law and order and public order is the price which the democracy in this country extracts from the public officials in order to protect the fundamental freedoms of our citizens. [910F H] 2. The continued detention of the detenu under the Act is not justified. It is well settled in our Constitutional framework that the power to directing preventive detention given to the appropriate authorities must be exercised in exceptional cases as contemplated in the various statutes dealing With preventive detention, and should he used with heavy deal of caution. There has to be awareness that of the fact necessitating preventive detention of a man for social Defence. If A man is being in custody, and there are no imminent danger of his release, the powers of preventive Detention should not he exercised. [936H; 910A B] Rameshwar Shaw vs District Magistrate Burdwan & Anr., ; and Ramesh Yadav vs District magistrate Etah and others, &, , relied upon. Rameshwar Shaw v District Magistrate, Burdwan & Ors., W.P. (Crl.) No. 2 96/86 dt 25.9.86 dt. 26.9 886; ; and Raj Kumar Singh vs The State of Bihar & Ors. Crl A. 353/86 with W. P. (crl) No. 27/86 dated 25 9.86.

The respondents were carrying on gold trade. These purchases were prohibited by the Central Government when he chooses to negative the request. While seeking permission under Section 28 of the Gold Control Act, 1968, he issued a notice on the respondents demanding its payment and penalty for the contravention of Section 28. The respondents contended that it offended section 28 in as much as no criteria or guide lines had been provided by reference to which the power conferred on the Administrator to refuse permission or grant permission should be exercised and that the section confers an arbitrary, uncanalised power upon the Administrator with the result that the licensed dealer was at his mercy while seeking permission to carry on money lending or banking business. Allowing the appeal and setting aside the judgment of the High Court in exercise of its discretion conferred on him under Section 27(6) in several of its clauses referred to certain concepts which Administrator was required to take into account, and these concepts were regarded as indefinite, uncertain and vague. For instance under clause (a), the Administrator was authorised to have regard to the anticipated demand 'as estimated by him for the ornaments in that region but the expression 'anticipated demand ' was really vague and incapable of assessment leading to a great deal of uncertainty; similarly the expression `anticipating demand ' ' was obviously vague and capable incapable of being assessment leading or leading to great deal. The Government issued an order on July 24, 1969 and directed restoration of possession of the shops premises to the respondents. On July 24. 1969, the respondent filed an appeal in this Court by special leave against the judgment and order of the Delhi High Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 Section 28 confers an unguided and uncanalised discretion without any criteria for guiding the discretion of the Administrator. Further, the section does not provide nor is any rule brought to our notice which enjoins upon the administrator to give a hearing to dealer who seeks permission under this Section and give reasons in case he decides to refuse the permission. [955E] 1.2 The object in putting the Act on the Statute Book as indicated by its long title is "to provide, in the economic and financial interests of the community for the control of production, manufacture, supply, distribution, use or possession of, and business in, gold ornaments and articles of gold and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto. " In the absence of parity of situation or circumstances the doctrine of parity cannot be invoked. [990C E] Harakchand Ratanchand Banthias vs Union of lndia, ; , applied. 959 2.1 The restrictions which have been imposed in section 28 are meant to prevent the circumvention of other provisions of the Act. Therefore, in view of the objective, the policy and the Scheme of the Insurance Act together with the necessity to ensure prevention of circumvention by the other provisions is afford more than sufficient guidance to the Administrator in the matter of exercising his discretion under that section. [989C E].

The appellants, who were the trustees of a Pachai Kandai Udayavar Temple in Madras, sought declaration to restrain respondents 1 to 3 from interfering with their possession of the properties. Their plea was that they had acquired title by prescription and the same was not a grant in favour of the religious endowment within the meaning of the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act (X of 1951). The Trial Court negatived the contention of the appellants that the properties in suit were alienated from time to time, and as such the plaintiffs ' title to the lands remained unaffected by the resumption proceedings. Held:(i) A person aggrieved by an alienation made by his predecessor is not bound by the conduct of others but is bound by it for a good cause which objections must be taken before he can claim that the property belonged to him and not to the religious wakf. In such a case, article 134 B does not permit such a plea to be raised. Column 1 of article 134 C provides for suits brought by servants other than those who are acting as de facto managers of a temple in regard to them, save as to specific property proved to have been vested in him for a specific object. The character of the representations made by previous manager in regard thereto was irrelevant for the purpose of article 133 B. (ii) A transferee has no title in the property and he is not entitled to any relief against that alienation or attachment. (iii) Even on the application of Art 134 B, the decision of the High Court is erroneous because on the facts proved it clearly shows not only that the alienor disposed of all the property but also that for the last 25 years or so, the management has been taken over by other persons who are working as de jure managers of the temple. This position has remained uninterrupted even after the passing of the Amending Act 1 of 1929.

[583C D] 4. When a agency has been created by the Government, it cannot be said that it can be said on the facts and circumstances of the case that the licensing authori ty had no jurisdic tion or power to suspend it. The appellants, who were displaced persons entered into an agreement with them, and had been put in possession of the mills and the factory on 31 8 1952. The respondent issued a notice to the appellants stating that they had systematically committed breach of various terms on which the properties bad been leased to them, calling upon them to show cause why the lease should not be cancelled and the lease might be cancelled. Thereupon the appellants filed an application before the Custodian under section 12 of the , and produced certain documents in support thereof. The Custodian applied for writs of prohibition restraining the respondent from taking any further action pursuant thereto which was allowed by the Custodian, but it was held that the notice had not been given to the respondent on the ground that, (i) the property in question had become the property of the appellant and therefore the cancellation of the lease was ultra vires the powers of the Custodian thereunder; and (ii) that the provisions of section 12 were not attracted to the case. The High Court held that on the plain language of section 8 it would apply whenever there was a lease, and quashed the notice. Held:(i) Under the circumstances of the case the rights of the appellants in so far as they related to the purchase by them of the Mills and the company were left open to the determination of the appropriate authorities, and that nothing in this decision should be reconciled with the contention of the petitioners that it confers no authority on him to go back upon his own contracts. (ii)(a) The right of the appel lants to move the Custodian is not cut down by section 12. It is for the first time in the arguances that those rights are sought to be agitated, and nothing in our decision should he taken as a pronouncement on those rights; it will be sufficient if the Custodian had the power under section 10 to cancel the lease in favour of the con cerned persons or that could be exercised "notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force." Held further, (a) Under section 12 an evacuee can move the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution against the order of the High court if it is satisfied that there was some breach of the terms on his part. Aswini Kumar Ghosh vs Arabinda Bose ([1952] , and Mesbolakram V. Bhimas Vaishya (A.I.R. , relied on. (b) Under that section no power can be exercised by a Custodian against the evacuees but an order of cancellation has to be made in accordance with the statute. In the present case there is nothing on record which would justify such a view, as there was also no material to justify any such action being taken in pursuance thereof, and therefore a notice under section 11 of the Act was not ultra vires.

The appellant, a minor son of Raghubir Singh had migrated to Rajasthan. The Sub Divisional Officer determined the ceiling area but an appeal preferred by Raghubir Singh was dismissed by the Commissioner. Thereafter Raghubir Singh filed a revision application under Section 230 of the Act before the Board. The revision application and the revision were rejected by the Revenue Appellate Authority, Bikaner on 6th September 1976. Then Raghubir Singh made another petition to the High Court for settingaside that part of the Sub Divisional officer 's order which had gone against the State and in his favour. It was contended on behalf of Raghubir A and his son that the power of general superintendence and control over all revenue courts vested in the Board could not be exercised to the detriment of the writ petitioners much less by way of suo motu exercise of powers. The appellant was a monthly tenant of the suit premises since about 2nd February, 1965. On or about 9th of February,1965, the respondent wanted to charge more rent or mesne profits for the period of 5 years from 1st September, 1965 till 31st of August, 1970; and it was further stated that the licensee had agreed to use the said premises as above and merely for the purpose of workshop business. The licensor gave and granted his 'leave and licence ' to the appellant on the licence to use and occupy the said demised premises for a period of five years from January 1st, 1969 till 31th August, 1971; that the agreement was being executed. It was alleged that this agreement was entered into between the parties since the respondent required to charge higher rent or rent profits. This agreement was in writing and this was for a term of 5 year, i.e., from 1 st September 1965 to 31st August 1970; that it was agreed by the licensor that if he committed any default of any terms and conditions or fails to pay the compensation for two months or if the licensee at any time puts up false or adverse claim of tenancy or sub tenancy the licensor shall be entitled to terminate the agreement and revoke and withdraw the permission granted earlier; but the licensor had agreed that if after the recovery of the permission a suit for possession could have been instituted under section 41 of the Bombay Rent Act, the licensor would be entitled lo terminate the said agreement and cancel and revoking the leave and licence granted earlier. The appellant claimed that he was a direct tenant of a shop premises since a period from 1 November, 1965 to March 31st, 1966; and that the licensor 's right was not affected by any breach of any of the terms and Conditions; and the respondent was not claiming protection as a sub tenant under the Rent Act but only the subtenancy as such. This contention was negatived by the Small Causes Court. The High Court allowed the revision on the ground that the licence was not put an end to by the appellant and that in any event, by filing the application for eviction the appellant licensor had granted an implied licence to the respondent. Allowing the appeal by special leave the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 It is well settled that a person continuing in possession of the premises after termination, withdrawal or revocation of the licence continued to occupy it was a trespasser or a person who had no semblance of any right to continue in occupation of the said Premises after revocation of it and was still liable to pay compensation or damages for its use and occupation. In order to go back to the setting of events, the appellant filed an application under section 115 C.P.C. in the High Court of Bombay under Article 227 of the Constitution. The respondent approached the High court under Article 228 of the constitution. The plea of protection was negatived on the said ground. [1061F] 1.2 In order that to get the advantage of section 15A of the Act, a person continues in possession after termination of the license and if permission to use land without exclusive possession was alone granted, a licence was the legal result. [ 1062H; 1063B] 1:3 The present case is governed by the Judgment of this Court in D.H. That decision is an authority on the subject. It is true that in order to get its advantage of Section 15A, the occupant must be in occupation or occupation of such premises after revocation as a licensee was coupled with an interest in the property, the agreement would be construed not as a mere licence but as a lease; it would also be for business purposes.

The State of Rajasthan was formed by Covenant entered into on February 28, 1948. The United State of Rajpur became the Part B State of Bikaner with effect from April 7, 1949. As a result of political changes it merged in Rajasthan now ; the United State became the part of Rajasthan. The State continued all the old laws till they were repealed or altered by the new State. It was common ground that when the United States came into existence on April 7. 1949 it provided for the continuance of all laws till them were repealed and there was specific provision in each Covenant that the assets and liabilities of the Covenanting States should be the assets, assets and the liabilities of their new States, throughout this process of integration from 1948 to 1950 must be regarded as invested with the character of an act of State and no claim based thereon could be enforced in a court of law. The respondent contended that the agreement did not bind the Union of India and therefore did not fall within the Category 'c ' of section 295(2) of the Indian Constitution; he was entitled to refund of the proportionate export duty for the quantity of 10,427 maunds and 20 seers which he could not export; Held, that there was recognition of the rights by the old sovereign throughout this period by taking over the assets which were altered or modified under the covenant in question and in view of that basic difference between that case and the present case. The agreement did expressly recognise the right of the subjects of the old States flowing from the old law and was not to be regarded an interim Constitution, but there was no recognition by the Union having been recognised by it throughout the process of merger. Dalmia Dadri Cement Co. Ltd. vs State of Saurashtra [1959] S.C.R. 710 and Dalmia Dadri cement Company Ltd. ([1959] Supp. S. C. R. 869) referred to. Dalmia tactics Dadri Cement Company case(1) is not applicable in the present cases as there was a competent law which clearly negatived the recognition of such an agreement and did not violate article 295(3). Dalmia Dadri Sugar Co. vs The State of Orissa ([1959) S.L.R., section C. D. 421), relied on.

The prosecution case was that on seeing the assault she called out to the accused not to beat him but they "reported" it to the police who arrested them and proceeded with the murder. The Sub Inspector who wrote out the First Information Report after ascertaining from the police that there were five persons in their possession, sent a report stating that (1) Tukaram struck Ramchander on his cheek; and (2) that he had an axe with axes and sticks. The trial court accepted this statement and convicted all of them for the murder but acquitted the appellants under section 302 I.P.C. as well as section 307, I. P. C., On appeal by special leave to appeal the High Court held that the conviction should be maintained but was upheld in respect of other two sets of committal proceedings which were heard jointly by a third Judge and not by the one who had convicted the appellants. Held: (i) In an appeal against acquittal under ss. 302 I P.C., it is well established that a common intention presupposes prior concert. Several persons can simultaneously attack a man and each can have the same intention, namely, the intention to kill. Therefore, when a person calls on bystanders to help him killing a given individual and they, either by their words or their acts indicate their assent to it and join him in the assault. It is only such evidence that he could be convicted of murder even if it be accepted that the deceased aimed a blow, at, out of which he had no hand from what the other three did. He can simultaneously inflict a separate fatal blow and yet none could be vicariously convicted for the act of any of the others; and if the prosecution cannot prove that his separate blow was a fatal one he cannot be convicted under section 326 I. K. C. vs Emperor, A.I.R. 1946 P C 45, referred to. (ii) In the present case there is no evidence of any prior meeting. It only relies on Rasikabai and Subhana for determining the fact Bhilia was directly charged with the crime and the injury which caused death was the one on the neck. (iii) The injuries found proved did not warrant a inference Of common intention in Pandurang 's case that there had once been a dacoity at Ramchaunder 's house and that he suspected "the accused" and reported them to the Police who arrested him, but nothing came of it, and they were later released. In the absence of anything specific, no conviction could be held on this account also.

The petitioner who was employed in the Central Public Works Department under the Ministry of Works and Housing, filed a Writ Petition before this Court contending that for retirement he had completed the age of 50 years on 10.2.1972 as prescribed by Fundamental Rule 56(j)(i) which provided: "Notwithstanding anything contained in this rule, the appropriate authority shall, if it is of the opinion that it is in the public interest so to do, have the absolute right to retire any Government servant by giving him notice of not less than three months in Writ or three months pay and allowances in lieu of such notice; (i) if he is in Class I or Class II service or post (and had entered Government serv ice before attaining the age Of fifty years), after he has attained the ageof 55 years, he shall retire from service with effect from the forenoon of 3rd November 1976, or, from the date of expiry of three months computed from the year of expiry thereof; and (ii) if in Class 1 or Class 11 service or Post (and having entered Government Service before attaining 26th May 1971) after he had attained the said age of fifty years, a person who has been appointed de novo may begin his service on an officiating basis or on a tempo rary basis and it is obvious that he has no right to the post and cannot therefore be so compulsorily retired by exercising the power under Rule 56 (j)(I). In further writ petitions, this Court directed the respondent Union of India vs K.R. Tahiliani and Anr. [1980] 1 SLR 847. The petitioners also prayed for a direction for payment of salary and allowances admissible under the rules on 30th January 1976 and 29th February 1976 respectively. Dismissing the Writ Petition, HELD: 1.1 Sub clause (iia) of Rule 56 of the Fundamental Rules as well as the power to compulsorily retire a public servant have been upheld by this Court. [616A] 1.2 There is no warrant for the conclusion that officiating Government servants in Class l or Class ll service or posts are outside the purview of sub clause (i). The possibility of such incumbent being sent back to the substantive post is not germane to the exercise of power contained in F.R 56. [ 634B C] 1:3 Where an officer belonging to a class I or class II service and Class II or service or service on regular basis has to be retired compulsorily, Rule 56 PG NO 836(j) comes to the rescue of the Government. But if he was only a temporary hand, he has not no right lo the post. [ 635C] 1 :4 The purpose of Fundamental Rules 56(J) is to confer power on the appropriate authori ties to compulsorily retired Government servants, in the Public interest and the classification of Govern ment servants into two categories and sub clause(i) takes within its sweep those Government servants who at the relevant time are in Class IIor Class II Service or post at the relei nt, whether substantively, temporarily or on officiating basis.

The respondents filed a suit in the Subordinate Court of Masulipatam against the appellant Corporation for recovery of Rs. 50,000 on 11th January, 1964 and Rs. 220 respectively in favour of the appellant as first premium. cheque was encashed by the appellant on 29th December, 1960. The widow of the deceased respondent No. 1 filed a plaint on 10th January 1964, which was allowed by the Subordinate Judge against the appellants. Subsequently, there was correspondence between the parties with regard to the medical examination and proposal circles and the connected papers of the present case and statements furnished by the Divisional Office to the Zonal office showing the new business in the year 1960 and proposals register work of Divisional office for the year 1961. The appellants filed a civil miscellaneous petition praying that in the circumstances stated in the affidavit filed therewith the High Court might be pleased to direct the Life Insurance Corporation to produce certain documents viz., proposal, review slips and proposalchea and the allied papers of this case and statement furnished by them was not accepted. In the written statement it was denied that the payment of the first premium amounted to acceptance of the proposal and the allegation about the assurance given to the deceased as alleged in the plaint was not true nor the alleged assurance if any, valid under law. It was further stated that the statements in the civil miscellaneous application that the respondents had cashed the above two cheques and appropriated the amounts and credited these in the account towards premium payable for the proposal were false. It is stated that on the death of the respondent No 1, the amount covering two cheques was lying in the deposit and in the suspense account of the Corporation and was not adjusted towards the premium since the proposal was not considered, the terms of acceptance were not fixed and the premium amount required for the proposals was not calculated. The Trial Court held that there was no concluded contract between the deceased and the Corporation. The trial court also noted that it was significant that the case set out in the plaints and the basis of the claim made in the notices sent to the Corporation was not that the proposal Was as a matter Of fact accepted by the Zonal Manager, on the other hand, claim was that it should be deemed to have been accepted. On appeal by the appellants before the High court also filed civil miscellaneous petitions praying that such a direction may be issued directing the Life insurance Corporation to produced certain documents namely proposals, review slip and proposal laboratories and the documents submitted to them. The High Court on hearing the parties held after considering the standing order exhibit B 13 and the various documents produced for the first time on record that there had been acceptance of proposal and like other contracts, the contract of insurance was complete by offer and acceptance. On behalf of the appellants it was contended that there is no concluded insurance contract between both the deceased & respondent Corporation and therefore, the Insurance contracted commenced on 11 th January, 1961 being the date of receipt of the balance towards premium by the Corporation in regard to certain other cases where only the Assistant Divisional Manager made similar endorsement. It could not be said that the acceptance of proposals was voluntary or intended to deprive the appellant of his liability for the same. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, ^ HELD: 1. When an insurance policy becomes effective is well settled by the authorities but before we note the said authorities, it may be stated that it is clear that the expression "underwrite" signifies accept liability under '. The dictionary meaning also indicates that. (See in this connection the statement of law in Corpus Juris Secundum, Vol. XLV page 986) wherein it has been stated as: "The mere receipt and retention of premium until after the death or of applicant does not give rise to a contract, although the circumstances may be such that approval could be inferred from retention of the premium. The general rule is that the contract will be concluded only when the party to whom an offer is made says or does something to signify his acceptance".

The respondent Bank applied in the suit for an interim injunction restraining encashment of the letter of credit opened in favour of the appellant company. Before the trial court the Bank pleaded that it was not a final order and as such, it was competent to grant the certificate. The trial the High Court set aside the order passed by the trial judge. In appeal to this Court on behalf of the Bank it was contended that an order granting injunction did not determine the rights and obligations of the parties in relation to the matter in dispute in the plaintiff suit or proceeding; if after the order is made, the suit or proceedings still remains to be tried and the rights in disputes have to be determined. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The Bombay Prevention of Ex communication Act was enacted and one of the issues raised in the plaint was whether the order finally disposing of the rights of the respondents was final. The appellant was appointed as a clerk by the Panchayat Samiti in 1963, long before the Amending Act came into force. On January 21, 1974 he was promoted as a Head Clerk on an ad hoc basis. On March 14, 1975 a resolution was passed by respondent 3 regularising the post of Head Clerk. On April 1, 1975, the appellant was promoted to the post as a head clerk on an ex hoc basis in January 1974. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court of Punjab and Haryana asking that he should be absorbed as a Grade Clerk. The writ petition having been dismissed by the High Courts, the appellants have filed this appeal. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The acceptance by the Governor on April 25, 1973 was not bound to absorb him in the post in the Panchayat Establishment until he was absorbed in Government service. [737E F] Under section 14(4) of the Amending Acts the Government of Haryana notified the absorption of the appellant as a Clerk though, as stated earlier, he was working as a 1200 head clerk in the Loharu Panchayat Samiti. Though the appellant had the right to be considered for promotion but the question is one whether the Panchayat Samitis had the power to make appointments to the Panchayats. Since the appellant according to the terms and conditions of his service with the Panchayat was entitled to be consider for promotion to the Post of a Head clerk, his appointment as a Post Clerk prior to his absorption in Government Service had to be recognised and protected, despite the fact that such appointment was made after June 13, 1973 when the Amending amending Act came in force.
