In the writ petitions filed before this Court, it was contended that there was no justification for cancelling the written part of the recruitment examina tion. On behalf of the Respondents it was argued that when no defect was pointed out in regard to the written examination and the sole objection was confined to exclusion of a group of successful candidates in the written exami nation from the interview, it had been no justification to cancel the written parts of the ap plication. Dismissing the appeals, this Court HELD: When no defect is pointed out In regard to re ing the written examina tions and the mere sole objection is confined to the exclusion of another group of selected candidates in his written examination from the exami cation. The situation could have been appropriately met by setting aside the recruitment and asking for a fresh interview of all eligible candidates on the basis of the written and freshly held interview became eligible for selection. [126F G] 1:2 When no defects were pointed out, there was not justification for canceling the written portion of the appointment exami natory and driv ing the candidates to litigation. On the facts alleged it directed that the result of the Written Examination shall stand er sustained and shall form the basis for the interview part of recruitment and on the ground that the candidate who had better performance in the Written examination were not called and candidates securing lesser marks in the viva voce examina ge were not only called for re qualify but were also finally selected. [127A B] The State Public Service Commission should have been more careful in dealing with the matter so that four years in the process of recruitment would not have been lost and the public cause would not suffer, public time would not has been wasted in requiring re doing of what had once been done and the litigation could have be avoided.

On February 8, 1983 an order was issued by the Government of Andhra Pradesh stating that it had decided to reduce the age of superannuation of all Government employees, other than in the last grade Service from 58 to 58 years. Two notifications were issued in exercise of power conferred by the Proviso to Article 309 read with Article 313 of the Constitution which was appended to that order. The petitioners who had attained the age Of 55 years were retired as a result of the orders. Two Notifications issued in September, 1979 and September 17, 1983 both came into force on February 8. This Order was superseded by another Notification dated October 29, 1979. In June, 1979, another Circular No. 36 was issued stating that the age for compulsory retirement should be increased from 55 to 58; and that the Government had reviewed the situation arising out of the enhancement of the age from 55. The State Government decided on its own to increase the age upto 55 years, though it was earlier increased from 65 to 58, that, in some States in India the age applied of retirement benefits for all Services rendered by experienced and mature persons from Government service will result in grave detriment to public services of the State; and, therefore, there was no basis at all for reducing the age. Two sets of petitions on behalf of the Suraj Rao were filed before the Andhra Pradesh High Court challenging the validity of the two Notifications on the ground that there was abuse of power by the State Government in not giving any previous notice to the employees which would have enabled them to arrange their affairs on the eve of retirement; and (ii) The writ petitions were contested on behalf. The first ground of challenge to the reduction of the retirement age from 58 years to 55 was that the Standing Orders dealing with the determination of the conditions of service of the employees who had already attained the date of retirement, had not been given retrospective effect so as to empower the Government to alter those conditions to their prejudice and that, therefore the interests of justice would be served if the Government proposed to reduce them from 55 years. The second ground was that it was arbitrary, irrational, and unconnected with the object which it sought to achieve. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: The amendment to the Fundamental Rules by Notification dated September 17 of 1983 is beyond the powers of the rule making authority or the legislature. By that amendment, a proviso was added to Rule 2 which reads thus: "Provided that the rules shall not be modified or E; replaced to the disadvantage of any person already in service". By G.O. the Government decided in October 1979 that the old age for retirement should continue to be 58 years for the Central Government employees with the modification that the retirement should take effect from the afternoon of the last day of the month in which the employee attains the age on superannuation. It was, therefore. clear that the amendment made to the offending rules was with the powers conferred by Article 309, and, consequently, the amendment as introduced retrospectively is beyond its powers of Rule making authority. [605 H; 602 A C D] (a) The special powers contemplated in the proviso are binding on the Government and cannot be subjected to judicial review under Articles 226 and 227. It is well settled that the service rules can he framed by the executive or legislative authorities. But there is no provision in the Act which gives finality to them, nor does it authorise the Government, to alter them retrospectively so as not to affect their validity on any other grounds. [ 602 B] (b) The second contention of the petitioners was that Rule 2 of the Fundamental Recruitment Rules, whereby the proviso to rule 2 was deleted by its amending Notification dated November 27, 1957, is beyond his powers and cannot therefore be sustained because it is not arbitrary or unreasonable in the circumstances of the case; Besides, the point made by the appellants was concluded by a Constitution Bench decision of this Court in Moti Ram Deka vs State of Uttar Pradesh, ; [1984] 3 SCR p.C.

The appellants are dealers in the State of Haryana. He purchased certain raw materials inside the State without paying tax thereon, in view of the provision contained in section 24 of the Haryana Sales Tax Act, 1973 (the Act '). The Department alleged that the said purchases were not sales in the course of export outside India within the meaning of section 5(1) of the Act. This claim was rejected by the taxing authorities and the High Court in writ petitions filed before it affirmed the decision against the assessees as early as 25.11.1980 in C.W.P. 1227/80, which was also affirmed by a Division Bench later 2. The question involved for determination is whether the sales effected by the appellants from outside the State are sale exigible to tax under section 9(1)(b) of Haryana Sales tax Act 1973 (for short 'the Act). Some of these were registered dealers and furnish declaration forms prescribed under Section 24 of that Act. The department however, denied the relief on the short ground that the sales made by the assesses fall within one of the exempted categories set out in section 9 (1)(a) (ii) later clause (b) above was compre hensive enough to include cases of despatches by a dealer of the manufactured goods otherwise than by way of sale in the state or despatches the manufactured cipted goods to a place outside the state. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that although the sales were inter State sales chargeable under section 5 (1) but not under section 50(3) they were exempted from payment of such tax by reason of section 24(1). On the question: whether the words "disposes of" used in clause (a)(ii) and later, clause (bb) above were Exped to include case of despatching goods by a registered dealer for the purpose of sale or purchase of goods under Section 17(2) of that act. Dismissing the appeals and writ petitions, the Court HELD: 1.1 The words "or despatches" used by the legislature in section 5 of the Indian Income Tax Act should be deemed to have been deleted from the statute. [353E] 1.2 From the language of Section 9(i)(a)(iii) a clear distinction between sales failing under sub section (3) and those falling under sub sec tion (1), is made out in sub section 3. The expression 'turnover ' in sub clause (ii)(b), later, cl. (b), used in the proviso to clause (c), makes the clear contrast between sales falling under subsections (3). and those failing under subsection (1). [353F G] 1:3 In other words, the exemption under Section 9 (i) has to be restricted only to export sales falling within the scope of section 50 (1 ).[353C E] 1 :4 The definition also excludes from its purview "the sale proceeds of goods on which purchase tax is leviable under this Act". [352F G; 353A] C.S.T. Sirajuddin vs Commissioner of Income Tax, Madras, ; C.I.T., Sirajuddin 's case ; , followed.

In a suit relating to a flat in which the husband had housed the wife resulted in a consent decree which also settled the marital dispute. The appellant was married and the respondent divorced the appellant around July 1962. A suit relating lo a flat was filed by the respondent and a few years later, who separated from July 1962, passed away in 1956 to the appellant and also the shares of the Cooperative Housing Society which built the flat concerned. There was a clause in the compromise whereby the appellant declared that she had no claim or right whatsoever against the defendant or against any estate and the properties of the Defendant. The Magistrate held that the appellant was a subsisting wife and awarded monthly maintenance of Rs. 300/ for the son and Rs. 400/ for her child taking due note of the fact that the cost of living in Bombay, where the parties lived, was high, and that the respondent had provided residential accommodation to the appel lant. This order was challenged before the Sessions Judge by an appeal before the sessions judge. The High Court rejected the claim of the appeLants. Hence this appeal. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 Every divorce otherwise eligible is entitled to the benefit of maintenance allowance and the dissolution of the marriage makes no difference to this right under the current Code. [79C] 1.2 The plea that the liability to pay maintenance had ceased on account of the payment of mehar, it was section 127(3) (b) absolution from this obligation under section 125 towards a divorced wife except on proof of payment of a sum stipulated by customary or personal law whose quantum is more or less sufficient to do duty for maintenance allowance is satisfied. [81B] 1:3 The mandate of section 127 (3)(b) is manifestly to recognise the substitute maintenance arrangement by lump sum payment organised by the custom of the community or the personal law of the parties. There must be a rational relation between the sum so paid and its potential as provision for maintenance. To interpret otherwise is to stultify the project. Law is dynamic and its meaning cannot he pedantic but purposeful. The proposition, therefore, is that no husband can claim under section 127.(3)(a) abs resolution from this obligations under section maintenance towards a divorce wife except upon proof of payments of a certain sum stipulated in customary or Personal law whose entitlement is more and sufficient to 34 do duty 814 for maintenance allowances. [86E F] 1 :4 The appellant 's plea is his right to ignore the statutory covenant contained in section 127 of the Code. So he must deal with the dual sub heads of the third ground. [84G H; 86A] 2.

The property which was a part of an extent of land situat ed on Mount Road, Madras bearing door Nos. 2 and 3 and the rent for the premises was Rs. 150 per month. The second lease deed was dated 22.9. 1947 and related to Door No. 1 (which was then the sole proprietary concern of one of them selves, Ganshyamdas Girdhardas Girdherdas (G.G.) but was converted subsequently into a partnership concern of G.G., which was later into a Partnership concern of another company. In 1956, the Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC) stepped into the shoes of these two insurance companies and became the owner of the property. On 20.7.65, the LIC moved two applications viz; (i) for fixation of fair rent in respect of the premises which was agreed to be sold under both lease deeds dated 22nd September, 1947, and (ii) for a direction to the furnishing of certain documents. The Rent Controller rejected these applications on the ground that these were bona fide. On appeal by the tenants, the Appellate Court held that the tenants had jurisdiction to fix fair rent at Rs.2,399.03 per month in respect thereof and therefore, the claim was sustainable. Allowing the appeal of the tenants and setting aside the orders passed by the Rent Controller, this Court, HELD: (1) In order to decide whether the denial or claim is bona fide and if he records a finding to that effect, the landlord shall be entitled to sue for eviction by having his title adjudicated upon in a civil court but that the owner cannot have a similar right in the matter of recovery of rent which is basically a relief for which he has to approach a civil Court. [530H; 532A] (2) The Rent Control Act, as already pointed out, provides only a machinery for fixation and determination of fair or standard rent for premises. If the tenant denies the title of the landlord or claims right of permanent tenancy, the Controller shall decide whether denial or claimed is bona fides and if so, he should leave it to be decided by ordi nary civil courts in appropriate proceedings. [632C] (3) The Court of Small Causes is not competent to adjudicate upon questions of title merely because the question may have had to be considered by the rent tribunals as a collateral issue in deciding certain applications before them. A tenant shall not be evicted whether in execution of a decree or otherwise except in accordance with the provisions of this section or sections 14 to 16: Provided that nothing contained in the said section shall apply to a tenant whose landlord is the Govern ment: Provided further that where the tenant denied the title by the tenant, he shall be entitle to sue under sub 7.

The petitioner was a respondent who had not appeared before the court and sought to be impleaded as a party. He, however, could not be heard by the Court on his own admission. It was contended for him that he was not heard after the final gradation list was published, that his name could not have been considered after the provisional gradation list having been prepared and therefore the respondent could not heard by him; and that he should have been given an opportunity to do so. Allowing the appeal and setting aside the judgment and order of the Mysore High Court, this Court, HELD: (1) The petition must be dismissed. [829 B] Shankariah vs Ram Chand & Ant. ; , 224, applied. (2) In the present case, the petitioner admitted that the Mysore State Civil Services Integration Rules 1960 provided for filing of objections only against the preliminary provisional inter state seniority list and did not provide any provision for filing objections or appeal ing against the final inter state Seniority list as per Annexure 'B '. The Scheduled Castes & Veterinary Services of the respective States in which the petitioner was given, had retired. He is a respondent before the Court. Therefore, the principle recognised in Shankaria malah 's case, (supra) has no application to such a case. [863 C E] (3) A right to representation was recognised as existing at time when the list was still to be considered as not finalised presumably because some mistakes had crept in due to want of heating on two points. The petitioner had ample opportunity to make representation in respect of the two points con vided by him, and therefore, the respondent cannot be heard. Even a list purporting to be final can be vitiated by non observance of condi tions prece dent.

Prior to 1965, in the High Court of Allahabad, Secretaries were on a higher pay scale than that of Section Officers. They were in the pay scale of Rs. 160 320 as against the pay scales of Rs 120 300 to Section Officers, and they were in service of the State Government. Thereafter, pursuant to an invitation by the Union Public Service Commission for Promotion from Grade I, the Pay Commission recommended a pay scale slightly lower than that, of Section Officer. The Committee submitted a detailed report, which did not accept the claim of Bench Secretaries for giving them pay scales equal to Section officers or Private Secretaries and directed them to give them pay scale equal to section Officers or Private Secretary, holding that their duties are equivalent to Private Secretaries of Hon 'ble Judges and have demanded the same pay scale which is given to Superintendents i.e. it would be violative of the constitutional right of equal pay for equal work. The Government accepted the recommendations. Subsequently, these pay scales were raised to Rs. 300 450 and Rs. 5 15 715 respectively, in another case, with similar duties and responsibilities, and the State Govern ment in its letter dated February 1, 1973 recommended 10 names among the Bench Secretaries Grade I and II, who ultimately submitted its report, and on February 1.1973, the pay of the petitioners was fixed at par with Section Officers if not on higher scale, and that it would have been violative of their right to have equal pay scale for equal works. The High Court accepted the recommendation, but instead half heartedly, the Government appointed the Pay Commis sioner (1971 72) headed by Shri Ali Zahir. On February 1 1973, the State had constituted a Committee and recommended for them a pay scales slightly lower as that of section Officers.

The procedure for imposition of taxes is contained in section 129 of the Municipalities Act and section 133 of the Municipal Corporation. But in order, to 20 judge whether, on that account, the State legislature loses its competence to pass the impugned act of 1973, it is necessary that to have regard to the object and purpose of that legislation and to the relevant provisions thereof, under which Special Area Development Authorities are given the power to tax lands and building within their jurisdiction. [26G] The respondent 1 cannot impose a tax without following the procedure prescribed by sections 129 and 133 of Madhya Bharat Municipalities Act which were introduced by an amendment made after the enactment of section 69 (d) was inserted in the Act of 1973. The main contention of the appellant before the High COurt was that the termination was bad as it had not given three months notice to him or provide him any compensation which he did under section 20(1) of the Act and that the Government should have taken into account for the period during which the lease was granted. Held further, that once the lease is determined under the second proviso it cannot be said to have been given one month ' notice. Section 20(2) of that Act does not provide for compensation for termination of rights created before July 1, 1945 and the High Courts had no power to interfere with the decision taken by the State Government in exercise of powers conferred on it by section 67 (1) Of the Act. It is true that under the provisions of the two provisos the lease could be terminated at its option and unconditionally under proviso (iii) that can be done only if no conditions were laid down in the section itself.
